full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: The plaintiff presented the appeal against the decree dated 30-7-2000 passed by the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.1 at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 82 of 1997, which dismissed the suit.

2. On 28-5-95 the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 166 of 1995 for eviction of defendant No. 1 from the suit land measuring about 300 square yards with structures thereon comprising of Plot # 8, Road # 3 of Block # A at Section # 10 of Mirpur Housing Estate fully described in the schedule to the plaint. On increase of the valuation, the suit was, on transfer to the aforesaid Court of Subordinate Judge, renumbered as Title Suit No. 82 of 1997.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to SA recorded tenant Abdur Rashid Matabbor, an uncle of the appellant. The Government acquired the suit land along with other property for Mirpur Housing Estate. After requisition and acquisition the government did not take over physical possession and, as such, the suit land remained in the possession of said Abdur Rashid Matabbor till his death.

4. Abdur Rashid died leaving three sons namely, Abdul Mannan, Abdur Rahman and Abdul Karim. They settled the suit land along with other property with the plaintiff and delivered possession. The plaintiff also got allotment of the suit plot from the Government. At the time of delivery of possession defendant No. 1 was occupying the tin shed as a caretaker. He was allowed to continue as such. On 27-6-94 on behalf of Mirpur Housing Estate possession was also delivered to the plaintiff. After mutation of his name the plaintiff possessed the suit property by payment of rents, taxes, etc.

5. On 27-1-95, when the plaintiff asked defendant No. 1 to vacate for construction, defendant No. 1 refused and resisted. Hence the suit.

6. Defendant No. 1 alone opposed the claim of the plaintiff by filing a written statement while defendant Nos. 2 and 3 jointly supported the plaintiff on allotment.

7. Defendant No. 1 claimed that the suit as framed in the form and manner was not maintainable and also hit by provisions of Specific Relief Act. Defendant No. 1 was not evictable from the suit property.

8. His definite case was that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acquired the suit land for Mirpur satellite town. On the prayer of Mohammad Jabbar the suit plot was on 17-9-63 allotted to him and delivered possession. Said Jabbar made a tin shed and lived there with his family. On 11-2-75 Jabbar orally gifted the suit plot to defendant No. 1 and delivered possession. Since then defendant No. 1 possessed the suit land by opening a municipal holding and obtaining electric line, water line and gas connection and living therein with his family. He made three more tin sheds and let them out to tenants. The suit land was never allotted to the plaintiff. In the suit plot the plaintiff had no title.

9. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in their written statement stated that on 5-5-94 the suit land was allotted to the plaintiff. On 20-7-94 possession was delivered, On 19-10-95 lease deed was registered and on 23-4-95 name of plaintiff was mutated. Subsequently, as there was mistake in the allotment, residential plot was allotted and on 27-7-95 the lease deed was registered. Name of Jabbar Kadri could not be found in respect of the suit land. They claimed that the claim of defendant No. 1 was not correct.

10. The parties lead evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit.

11. The appellant has come up with an application under Order XXIII, rule 1(2) read with section 107 of the Code of Civil Procedure for withdrawal of the appeal as well as the suit with permission to sue afresh.

12. Mr Ozair Farook, learned Senior Advocate on behalf of the appellant, submits that the suit was poorly drafted by a Mofussil lawyer and forgot to pray for declaration of title in the suit land. He submitted that in the absence of such prayer the suit was doomed to fail and, in fact, failed;

13. Opposing the application, an affidavit was filed on behalf of respondent No. 1

14. Mr Md Nazibur Rahman, learned Senior Advocate for the respondent No. 1, submitted that after dismissal of the suit even on the question of title the application did not deserve consideration otherwise the plaintiff would be allowed to commence fresh litigation on the same cause of action. He took us through the judgment and submitted that learned Subordinate Judge already found that the plaintiff failed to prove his title, interest in the suit land.

<u>15. Following decisions were cited at the Bar for and against the prayer:</u>

<u>(a) Atul vs Rau Kishore, AIR 1956 Orissa 77; (b) Muhammad Din vs Atta Muhammad and others, PLD 1957 Lahore 971; (c) Modan Mohan Pal Annosatra vs Abdus Samad and others, 32 DLR 176; (d) Kabiruddin and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, 43 DLR (AD) 201; (e) Gurnek Singh and another vs Gurbachan Singh and others, AIR 1986 Panjab and Haryana 228 and (f) Md Abdul Quddus vs Md Mustafa Hossain 1992 BLD (AD) 131.</u>

16. Sub-rule 1 of rule 1 of Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure entitles a plaintiff to withdraw his suit or abandon part of his claim at any time after institution of the suit.

17. Such provision is now well settled to enable an appeilant as well to withdraw the appeal along with the suit.

18. Sub-rule 2 of rule I of said Order empowers a court to allow a plaintiff to institute a fresh suit for the same subject matter of a suit Or part of claim if it is satisfied that the suit would fail by reason of some 'formal defect' or for some 'other sufficient grounds.

<u>19. What is 'formal defect' has not been defined anywhere in the Code. But there are good authorities that the expression formal defect should receive wide and liberal meaning. Even when a plaintiff could not be allowed to Withdraw his suit with liberty to sue afresh on the ground of any 'formal defect' the Court may still allow him to do so on any other ground sufficient for satisfaction of the Court. The expression other sufficient grounds does not appear to have been used by the legislature as ejusdem generis with the expression formal defect.</u>

<u>20. The legal meaning of the word formal is done in due form or with solemnity; according to regular way. The expression, formal defect connotes defects of diverse kinds not affecting the merit of the case but arising out of some error made in good faith. It is a defect of form prescribed by the rules of procedure. If it goes to the root of the suit, it is not a formal defect. Even when there was no such formal defect the Court is not powerless to grant the same prayer if justice demands.</u>

21. So, ultimate discretion rests with the Court. the Court should only guard that the plaintiff should not be allowed another opportunity to commence a fresh trial after he failed to conduct the suit with care and diligence; (Madan Mohan Pal vs Abdus Samad 32 DLR 176).

22. If the suit was disposed of and ultimately dismissed on merits then the plaintiff would not be entitled to have the liberty to sue afresh on the same subject matter (Gurnek Singh and another vs Gurbachan Singh and others, AIR 1986 Panjab and Hariana 228.

23. In Atul vs Raukishore AIR 1956 Orissa 77, a suit was instituted for accounts but without any relief prayed for dissolution of partnership. A single bench found that failure of the Advocate to incorporate a prayer for dissolution of the partnership was bound to result in dismissal of the suit. That was a defect and provides a sufficient ground for permitting the plaintiff to come to the Court again with a properly drafted plaint.

24. In Muhammad Din vs Atta Muhammad, PLD 1957 (WP) Lahore 971, a single bench upheld the order of the trial Court allowing withdrawal of the suit on the reasoning that the omission in the plaint of the fact that the parties were governed by custom was not intentional. In the absence of such averment in the plaint, the plaintiff ran grave risk of being non-suited, The plaintiffs should not be made to suffer for the negligence of their Counsel in not drafting a proper plaint.

25. In lsmail vs Fida Ali, PLD 1965 SC 634 = 17 DLR (SC) 531 the Supreme Court of Pakistan on the oral prayer of the learned, Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent granted leave for withdrawal of the suit against the defendant with permission to file a fresh suit. The suit was based on endorsement simpliciter and the endorsement appeared on the back of a promissory note. The suit was found bound to fail in the form as framed. The suit was decreed by a single Judge.

26. On careful perusal of the plaint we find that learned Advocate could not be sure as to how to seek the relief in the facts and circumstances of the case. There is more than one amendment by both parties. Even thereafter, when in the written statement of the defendant No. 1 it was clearly claimed that the suit as framed was not maintainable and also hit by the provision of the Specific Relief Act it did not occur to him that he should seek a declaration of title. It is true that there is a finding on title by the trial Court but such finding must be taken to be incidental to the finding on the relief for recovery of possession only.

27. When the title of the plaintiff was seriously contested simple suit for eviction was doomed to fail. And seeking a decree of declaration of title, the plaintiff is required to state clearly the history of title as he could trace.

28. In the circumstances, we are of the view if the appellant is not allowed to sue afresh for a decree of declaration of title he would be deprived of an opportunity to vindicate his right to the property in question. The application therefore merits consideration.

29. In the result, the application is allowed. Consequently, impugned judgment and decree are hereby set aside. The plaintiff is allowed to withdraw the appeal with permission to sue afresh on the subject matter as prayed for.

Send down the records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant- petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the Title Appeal No. 26 of 1986 shall not be dismissed after setting aside the judgment and decree dated 1-4-1997 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Appeal No. 26 of 1986 affirming those dated 30-3-1986 passed by the learned Munsif, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 620 of 1981 should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

Short facts of the case are as follows:

2. The predecessor of the opposite parties No. 1 to 3, as plaintiff instituted the Title Suit No. 206 of 1974 in the Second Court of Munsiff, Dhaka, which subsequently being transferred to the Court of Munsiff, Gazipur was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 620 of 1981, against the petitioners and others as defendants, praying for establishment of title and recovery of Khas possession of the disputed property on the allegations, inter alia, that the suit land along with other lands originally belonged to one Raj Bihari Ghose, who died leaving 8 sons, and as per amicable partition made by them the suit land fell into the share of 5 brothers namely, Paresh Chandra, Jogesh Chandra, Ramesh Chandra, Urnesh Chandra and Gonesh Chandra; and that while the aforesaid 5 brothers were in possession of the same transferred the disputed land along with other lands to the plaintiff; that since purchase the plaintiffs had been possessing the same on payment of rent and mutated his name, and that SA and RS record were prepared in his name; that the defendant No.2 with an ill motive illegally and collusively by misleading the Enemy Property Authority took lease of the disputed property on 6-7-1970 in Enemy Property Case No. 60 of 1970; that the Enemy Property Authority has got no legal authority to lease out the said land in favour of the defendant No.2, as because the plaintiff is the sole owner of the land in question; and that on the basis of so-called lease the defendant No.2 forcibly dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land which created a cloud over the title and possession of the land in suit.

3. The defendant No.2, predecessor of the petitioners contested the said suit by denying the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable, hopelessly barred by law of limitation, no cause of action has arisen for the suit and hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, and that the disputed land belonged to Rash Bihari Ghose, who inducted the defendant No.2 in the disputed portion of the land and allowed him to live there by erecting houses, and accordingly he has been living with the members of his family (the present petitioners) in the disputed Plot No. 299 corresponding to RS Plot No. 375 by raising buts and structures thereon and has been possessing the land of the suit plot No. 298 corresponding to RS Plot No. 377 by cultivating and enjoying usufructs from the time of Rash Bihari Ghose; and he has been in possession of the disputed land for about 35 years, and that after the death of Rash Bihari Ghose his 3 sons Naresh Chandra Ghose, Dinesh Chandra Ghose and Suresh Chandra Ghose in whose share the disputed land fell also allowed the defendant No.2 to hold possession and live in the aforesaid manner; that the defendant No.2 is in possession of the entire disputed land measuring an area of 1.05 acres to the exclusion of all including the plaintiff and his vendors and predecessors; that the 3 sons of Rash Bihari Ghose namely, Naresh Chandra Ghose, Suresh Chandra Ghose and Dinesh Chandra Ghose left this country permanently for India in 1964 keeping the disputed land under the care and possession of the defendant No.2 The alleged predecessors of the plaintiff had never been in ownership and possession of the disputed land, that the disputed land has been declared enemy property and the Government granted lease of the disputed land along with other lands to the defendant No.2 in Enemy Property Case No.60 of 1970; that the plaintiff instituted a suit for permanent injunction in respect of 2.19 acres of land against the defendant of the present suit and others in the Second Court of Munsiff, Dhaka being Title Suit No.125 of 1970 asserting his possession and claiming the disputed land exclusively belonging to the 5 sons of Rash Bihari Ghose, their alleged predecessors, but even in that suit the witnesses of the plaintiff deposed in Court about the possession of this defendant for about 15/16 years before the institution of the said Title Suit No.125 of 1970, and, as such, dismissed the suit in respect of 0.05 acres of land possessed by the present defendant No.2 and rejected the prayer for injunction in respect thereof.

4. The plaintiff examined 2 witnesses and the defendant examined 3 witnesses in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsiff, Gazipur decreed the suit by her judgment and decree dated 30-6-1986.

5. As against that the heirs of defendant No.2 preferred Title Appeal No.26 of 1986 before the District Judge, Gazipur, and the same was heard on transfer by the Subordinate Judge, First Court, Gazipur, who dismissed the said appeal by his judgment and decree dated 6-4-1997.

6. Being aggrieved by the said appellate judgment and decree, the defendant-petitioners obtained the present Rule.

7. ABM Matiur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, placed the revisional application, the deposition of the PWs and DWs, the impugned judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below and submitted that though the plaintiff in his plaint stated that the cause of action of the suit arose on 6-7-1970, but in his deposition no date has been mentioned and nothing has been stated about the date of his dispossession from the suit land and, as such, the learned Courts below committed error in law in decreeing the suit and in dismissing the appeal. The learned Advocate further submitted that in a suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession, the plaintiff must prove his date of possession and dispossession in order to show that the suit is not time-barred, but the plaintiff in his deposition having failed to mention the date of dispossession, the Courts below ought to have held that the plaintiff failed to prove his cause of action in filing the suit and, as such, the suit is barred by limitation.

8.	None appears to oppose the Rule.

9.	On perusal of the judgment passed by the learned trial Court, it appears, no issue has been framed regarding limitation. The learned trial Court on consideration of the evidence and materials on record found that the plaintiff could prove his title in the suit land; that title of the defendant cannot be declared for some portion of ejmali property of enemy property without effecting partition and, as such, the order of lease in that respect is not sustainable in law. The learned trial Court further found that PW 1 admitted that the defendant No.2 (the predecessor of present petitioners) has been in possession of the suit land as per permission of Rajbihari and that he/they may be ousted at any time by the owner of the land in question. The learned trial Court further found that the defendant- petitioner being an early lessee and, as such, there is no bar in decreeing the suit against the defendant. It appears, the learned trial Court did not consider the deposition of the plaintiff PW 1 regarding possession and dispossession and also there is no finding by the learned trial Court to that effect.

10. On appeal, by the defendant petitioners, it appears; the learned appellate Court also held that the plaintiff could prove his title in the suit land. The learned appellate Court it appears, did not consider the deposition of the PWs and DWs on record at all, but held that the learned trial Court elaborately discussed all the issues and there is no illegality or error in law committed by the learned trial Court in decreeing the suit.

<u>11. The established principle of law is that in a suit for declaration of title and for recovery of possession, the plaintiff must prove his cause of action, in other words, his possession in and dispossession from the suit land in order to prove that the suit is within time. Reference may be given to the case of Fatema Khatoon vs Narasing Jiew Idol reported in 7 BLC 6, but in the present case, it appears, the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court did not consider the question of limitation as well as the question whether plaintiff was able to prove the cause of auction for filing the suit. Moreover, the learned appellate Court being the last Court of fact it was mandatory on the part of the learned appellate Court to consider the evidence of PWs and DWs on record, but the learned appellate Court did not consider the deposition of the PWs and DWs on record and it affirmed the judgment of the trial Court holding that the learned trial Court elaborately discussed all the issues in the suit.</u>

12. I have gone through the deposition of the PWs and DWs on record, it appears, PW I in his examination-in-chief stated nothing about the date of dispossession of the plaintiff by defendant from the suit land. The plaintiffs case is that the defendant dispossessed him on 6-7-1970 from the suit land but the case of the defendant is that the defendant's predecessor Vomar Bepari has been in possession of the suit land for last 40 years by having homestead in the suit land and that this fact has been admitted by the PWs 1 and 2 in their deposition, though the case of the plaintiff is that the defendant No.2 is in permissive possession of the predecessor of the plaintiff in the suit land. Thus it shows that the question of possession and dispossession of the plaintiff in the present case is very much material but the Courts below did not consider and give any finding of this important legal aspect of the case and, as such" in my opinion, it is a gross omission on the part of the Courts below, especially on the part of the learned appellate Court, while dismissing the appeal by the impugned judgment and decree calling for interference by this Court in revision.

13. Furthermore, it appears, from the deposition of the PWs and DWs that the defendant and his predecessor had been in possession of the suit land since much before filing the suit and, as such" in my opinion, the learned appellate Court committed error in law in dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment passed by the learned trial Court and, as such, the same are liable to be set aside.

14. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost and the judgment and decree passed by the Court below are set aside and Title Suit No. 620 of 1981 is hereby dismissed.

15. The order of status quo granted at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the LC Records immediately.

End.

full_judgment:
Obaidul Hassan J: This appeal is directed at the instance of the defendant-appellants against the judgment and decree dated 25-9-2004 (decree signed on 26-9-2004) passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Noakhali in Title Suit No.25 of 2004 decreeing in the suit as alternative dispute resolution.

2. The respondent Nos.1 to 7 as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 25 of 2004 impleading the appellant as defendant No.35 with other 37 defendants for declaration' of title in the suit land described in the schedule of the plaint.

3. It appears that on 15-8-2004 the learned Joint District Judge, Noakhali by his order appointed one Mr Moinuddin Ahmed Khasru, an Advocate of Noakhali District Court as Mediator and fixed 31-8-2004 for the report from the Mediator. Thereafter, on 31-8-2004 defendant Nos. 16 to 24, 29 to 31, 37 and 38 filed a compromise petition before the Court and on the same date defendant No. 35, the present appellant, by filing an application prayed for time to file their written statement. Subsequently, on 25-9- 2004 the application filed by the defendant No. 35 was rejected and on the same date the compromise petition filed by the defendant Nos. 16-24, 29-31, 37 and 38 was accepted and the suit was decreed on the basis of alternative dispute resolution and made the compromise petition as a part of the decree.

4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Noakhali the defendant No. 35 being appellant has preferred this appeal.

5. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant submits that the order dated 15-8-2004 was passed in absence of the defendants which is contrary to the provision of section 89A(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Because in the said section it has been mentioned that the decision for mediation should be taken in presence of the parties in person or represented by their respective pleaders, but in this case the learned Joint District Judge passed the order in absence of the defendants, as such the said order was passed illegally. He further submits that subsequently on 31-8-2004 the present appellant filed an application for allowing him to contest the suit by filing written statement, the learned Judge in the trial Court rejected their prayer and accepted the compromise petition filed by the other defendants and decreed the suit on the basis of compromise petition filed by the other defendants. Since appointment of the mediator was illegal, the judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside. Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury further submits that during the proceeding no registered process was sent to the address of the present appellant which is required by law to do. As such the impugned judgment and decree is liable to be set-aside.

6. Mr Md Waliur Reza Chowdhury along with Mr. Musharraf Hossain Mazumder learned Advocates appeared on behalf of the respondents. Mr. Musharraf Hossain submits that section 89A (12) is a clear bar for the parties to prefer any appeal or revision against the judgment or any order or decree passed by the Court and as such the present appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submits that in fact the judgment and decree passed against the present appellant ex parte, thus he (defendant No. 35) could have filed an application before the Court under Order IX, rule 13 for setting aside the ex parte decree but without exhausting that forum, the appellant has preferred this appeal which is clearly barred by sub-section 12 of section 89 A of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

7. In reply to the argument advanced by Mr Mosharraf Hossain learned Advocate for the appellant, Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury submits that since the appellant was not a party to the settlement he has every right to prefer appeal against the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. He further submits that since on 31-8-2004 in his presence decree was passed there was no any scope for the appellant to file any application before the trial Court under Order IX, rule 13.

8. We have gone through the judgment and decree perused the other relevant papers and we have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates and also gone through the provisions of law.

9. As per section 89A (1) the trial Court can only pass an order for mediation in order to settle the dispute or disputes in the suit in presence of the contesting parties in the Court in person or by their respective pleaders. The provision of section 89A (1) of Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:

"Except in a suit under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 (Act No. 4 of 1990), after filing of written statement, if all the contesting parties are in attendance in the Court in person or by their respective pleaders, the Court may, by adjourning the hearing, mediate in order to settle the dispute or disputes in the suit, or refer the dispute or disputes in the suit to the engaged pleaders of the parties, or to the party or parties, where no pleader or pleaders have been engaged, or to a mediator from the panel as may be prepared by the District Judge under subsection (10), for undertaking efforts for settlement through mediation:

provided that, if all the contesting parties in the suit through application or pleadings state to the Court that they are willing to try to settle the disputes in the suit through mediation, the Court shall so mediate or make reference under this section."

10. From the record it appears that on 15-8- 2004 learned Judge of the trial Court passed the order in absence of the defendants, not only the present appellant but also in absence of the other defendants. The extract of the order runs as follows:

“অধ্য মোকদ্দমা ইস্যু গঠন ও বিবাদীদের বর্ণনার পোষকে কাগজপত্র  দাখিল এর জন্য দিন ধার্য্য  আছে। বাদী পক্ষ হাজির। বিবাদী পক্ষ হাজির নাই।

দেখিলাম।

মামলাটি দেওয়ানী কার্য্যবিধি সংহিতায় ধারা 89A(1) অনুসারে MEDIATION মাধ্যমে  নিস্পত্তির প্রচেষ্টা গ্রহণের জন্য  জনাব মাইনউদ্দিন আহম্মেদ  খসরু এ্যাডভোকেট সাহেবকে মধ্যস্থকারী (MEDIATOR) নিযুক্ত হইল।

বিজ্ঞ MEDIATOR বরাবরে পত্র পেরণ করা হউক।

ইং ৩১-০৮-২০০৩ তারিখ MEDIATOR এর প্রতিবেদন  দাখিলের জন্য নির্ধারণ করা হইল।”

11. From the order it appears that the same was passed in absence of all the defendants. In our opinion as per section 89 A sub-section-1 of the Code of Civil Procedure this order was not sustainable in the eye of law. It appears also from the record that on 31-8-2004 the compromise petition was filed by the other defendants and the defendant No. 35-the present appellant filed an application for adjournment of the hearing to enable him to file a written statement,' but from the order dated 25-9-2004 we find that the application of the appellant-defendant No. 35 was rejected saying that the defendant No. 35 intentionally avoided the case and intentionally did not appear to the Court. On the same date the learned Joint District Judge ordered that the compromise petition filed by the other defendants are accepted and the suit be decreed, making the contents of the compromise petition as part of the decree.

12. Since the present appellant even could not file the written statement and even he was not allowed to file a written statement, he preferred this appeal. The submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the appellant to the effect that he had no scope to file any application under Order IX, rule 13 is correct, because on 25-9-2004 the decree was passed in his presence. Since it was passed in his presence he had no scope to file any application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

13. Now the question whether sub-section 12 of section 89 A of the Code of Civil Procedure is a bar for any party to prefer any appeal against such a decree where he was not a contestant. Before entering to the discussion let us see what does law say. Sub-section 12 of section 89A of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:

"No appeal or revision shall lie against any order or decree passed by the Court in pursuance of settlement between the patties under this section."

<u>14. It appears from the wordings of this sub- section that the legislature has enacted this law to bar the parties from preferring any appeal or revision against any decree or order, who were the par- ties of settlement. The parties, who entered into the settlement in pursuance of the order passed by the Court by a mediator, cannot file any appeal or revision before any higher forum against such a decree or order passed, by any Court. But in our opinion either of the party defendant or appellant, if not a party to the settlement, can prefer appeal or revision to the higher forum. Sub-section 12 of section 89A will not be applicable in the case of any party, who are not the party to the compromise in pursuance of settlement under this section.</u>

15. Section 89 A has been inserted in the Civil Procedure Code vide Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act IV of 2003 to encourage the litigant people to settle their dispute through Meditation. Perhaps to give total effect of this new provision of law the legislature has imposed this restriction from preferring any appeal or revision against a decree passed through mediation by the parties of the settlement.

16. In the present case we find that appellant, (the defendant No. 35) filed an application for allowing him to submit written statement to contest the suit, but he was not allowed and, subsequently the suit was decreed on the basis of alternative dispute resolution and thus we are of the opinion that the defendants who were the parties of the settlement, are not entitled to prefer any appeal or revision, but the present appeal is very much maintainable as the appellant was not a party to the settlement. Thus we are inclined to allow this appeal, setting aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 25 of 2004. We are also inclined to send the case back on remand.

17. Accordingly the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and decree dated 25-9-2004 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No. 1, Noakhali in Title Suit No. 25 of 2004 are set aside and the case is sent back on remand to the Court where the suit was pending. If the presiding Judge of that Court who passed the decree is still in that Court, he will not hear the case. In that event he will send the case to the learned District Judge, who will take steps for transferring the case to a Court of competent Jurisdiction who will hear and dispose of the matter in accordance with law.

Send down the lower Court records along with a copy of this judgment immediately to the Court concerned.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 4th day of March, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.162 of 1991).
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J. This appeal, by leave, is from the judgment and order dated the 4th day of March, 2009 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No.162 of 1991 dismissing the appeal.

<u>2. Short facts necessary to dispose this appeal are that respondent No.1 herein as the plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No.137 of 1986 in the Court of Subordinate Judge (now the Joint District Judge), Second Court, Chittagong for specific performance of contract impleading the present petitioners and one Gour Shankar Banik as principal defendant Nos.1 and 2 and the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong as pro-forma defendant. The suit was decreed ex-parte on 25.02.1987. Thereafter, the appellant who was defendant No.1 (hereinafter referred to as the defendant) filed an application in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Second court, Chittagong under Order a, rule 13 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) for setting aside the ex-parte decree alleging that the ex-parte decree was obtained by the plaintiff fraudulently without serving any summons upon him. He came to know about the ex-parte decree on 12.07.1987, when his daughter was resisted by the plaintiff from picking up guava from the guava tree situated on the bhiti of the suit land disclosing that he got the land by a decree from the said Court of the Subordinate Judge. The plain-tiff also threatened the defendant to leave the suit land, otherwise he could face serious consequences. On such disclosure of facts by the plaintiff, the defendant made an enquiry in the Court on 15.07.1987 and came to know definitely about the ex-parte decree and then filed the application for the relief aforementioned. The application was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.67 of 1987.</u>

3. The plaintiff - respondent (hereinafter referred to as the plaintiff) contested the miscellaneous case by filing written objection asserting that summonses of the suit were duly served upon the defendants including defendant No.1 and the Court being satisfied as to the service of summons upon the defendants fixed the suit for ex-parte hearing and eventually the suit was decreed ex-parte.

<u>4. At the time of hearing of the miscellaneous case, both the parties examined one witness each. The learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 26.06.1989 rejected the application on the finding, inter-alia, that the summons of the suit was duly served upon the defendant-petitioner on 19.09.1986 which was evidenced from the service returns of the summons. The process server gave a report to the effect that no having found the defendant present served the summons upon him personally by taking his signature. The learned Subordinate Judge further observed that since the summons of the suit was served upon defendant No.1 as per report of the process server, there could no be any doubt as t the service of summons of the suit upon him. The learned Subordinate Judge further observed that although the decree was passed against defendant Nos.1 and 2 defendant No.2 did not challenge the same by filing any miscellaneous case. The Court below further found that the application was barred by limitation as in support of the knowledge of the ex-parte decree of the suit by the defendant for the first time on 12.07.1987, no other witness was examined.</u>

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, the defendant filed First Miscellaneous Appeal No.29 of 1989 before the then Sessions of the High Court Division at Chittagong which having been transferred to the permanent seat in Dhaka was renumbered as Miscellaneous Appeal No.162 of 1991. A Division Bench of the High Court Division hearing the appeal by the impugned judgment and order dismissed the same. Against the judgment and order of the High Court Division, the appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.948 of 2009 before this Division and leave was granted by this Court giving rise to this appeal; the grounds are:

"I. For that having regard to the provisions of Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the issue in an application for setting aside ex-parte decree being that the summons was not duly served on the defendant or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing, and there being evidence on record of the defendant as PW-1 in the Miscellaneous Case No.67 of 1987 that he did not receives the summons of the suit and that the signature of the summons signifying the service on him was not his, and having regard to the fact that his evidence in this respect was not at all controverted by the evidence of the process server or any other witness, the High Court Division was wrong in holding that the trial Court committed no illegality in rejecting the Miscellaneous case filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter the High Court Division erred in law in not restoring the suit by allowing the FMA upon setting aside the ex-parte decree of the trial Court.

II. For that the plaint of the suit having shown the address of the defendant in a village at Mirersarai in Chittagong, and admittedly the summons, according to the process server's report, having been served at an address at Halishahar in Chittagong town which is given as the present address of the defendant "C/O: Dr. S.L. Muzumder, 557, Halishahar Road, Chatopol, P.S. Double Mooring, Chittagong" and the defendant in his deposition as P.W.1 in the Miscellaneous Case having categorically stated that he never lived at Halishahar, Chittagong and that did not know the witnesses named in the service return of the summons, the High Court Division erred in law in failing to hold that the summons of the defendant was not duly served and in that view of the matter the High Court Division was wrong in failing to hold that the defendant's evidence having satisfied that the summons was not served on him, the suit is liable to be restored upon setting aside the ex-parte decree and on such finding the FMA ought to have been allowed by the High Court Division."

6. Mr. Rokanudddin Mahmud, learned Counsel, for the appellant has, in fact, canvassed the grounds on which leave was granted.

7. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, has supported the impugned judgment and order on the sub-mission that the Appellate Court being the last Court of fact on comparison of the signatures of the defendant appearing in the summons in the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code and in the deposition sheet, came to the finding that all those, were of the hand of same person, i.e. the defendant, there is no point in agitating that the summons of the suit was not served upon him, no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and order and the appeal be dismissed.

8. From the application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code, it appears that the defendant categorically asserted that the summons of the suit was not served upon him and that he came to know about the ex-parte decree only on 12.07.1987 when his daughter was prevented from picking guava from the guava tree situated in the bhiti of the suit land and that he came to know that the ex-parte decree surely from the information slip dated 15.02.1987 filed in Court. The defendant asserted the said fact when he examined him as PW 1. He also asserted that the signature appearing in his name in the summons was not his and that he did not put any signature in the summons.

<u>9. It is by now a well settled legal principle that in case of allegation of non-service of summons made by the defendant, the onus is upon the plaintiff to prove the service of summons. In the instant case, admittedly the process server who allegedly served the summons upon the defendant was not examined. Not only was that none in whose presence the process server allegedly served the summons also examined. The plaintiff was examined as OPW 1. He stated in his cross-examination that he was not present when the summons was served upon the defendant. He further stated that the defendant did not sign the summons in his presence and that he did not know the persons who were present at the time of service of the summons (in the deposition sheet, in Bangla, it has been recorded as"</u>

<u>..............প্রার্থিক বাদীর উপর সমন জারী করার সময় উপস্থিত ছিলাম না।</u>

<u>প্রার্খিক বিবাদী সমন দরখাস্ত আমার সামনে করে নাই সমন জারীর সময় আর কে কে উপস্থিত ছিল জানি না। প্রার্থিক বিবাদী সনে দস্তখত আমার সামনে করে নাই।”)</u>

<u>10. So, OPW1 cannot be accepted as a witness to the service of summons upon the defendant. In this regard, it is also necessary to state that OPW1 in his examination-in-chief stated that the defendant after coming from India used to live at Halishahar, Chittagong town (which fact was denied by PW 1) and the summons of the suit was served upon the plaintiff at his Halishahar address, so the onus was upon the plaintiff to prove that actually the defendant lived at Halishahar than his village address, but he failed to discharge the said onus. It further appears that in the plaint, two addresses of the defendant were shown, one his village address at village-Dewanpur, Upazila-Mirersharai, District-Chittagong and the other at 557, Halishahar Road, Chatopol, P.S. Double Mooring, Chittagong under the care of one Dr. S.L. Muzumder, but the summons of the suit was allegedly served at the address of Halishahar only, i.e. no summons was served at the village address of the defendant. It is also very pertinent to state that the suit property is in village-Dewanpur, Police Station -Mirersharai (as evident from the schedule to the plaint), so it was natural that the summons of the suit would be served at his village address. The defendant in his deposition categorically stated that it was not correct that he used to stay at Halishahar, Chittagong town and that his house was not at Halishahar. None was examined from Halishahar to prove that the defendant actually lived at Halishahar address. In this regard, it is also very important to state that the defendant in his application under Order IX, rule 13 mentioned only one address, i.e. village-Dewanpur , Upazila-Mirersharai, so it was more obligatory upon the plaintiff to show that the defendant actually used to live at Halishahar under the care of one Dr. S.L Muzumder, 557, Halishahar Road, Chatopol, P.S. Double Mooring in which address the summons of the suit was allegedly served. Our common sense failed to see any reason to mention an address of the defendant in the plaintiff under the care of some body in a town, when the suit property is situated in a village. And then again why the summons of the suit should be served at the temporary address in the care of some body without serving the summons at the permanent village address where the suit property is situated and this speaks a volume and lends prima-facie support to the case of the defendant that the ex-parte decree was obtained fraudulently without serving any summon upon him, but neither the learned Subordinate Judge not the High Court Division considered these apparent factual and legal aspect of the case and thus fell into an error in taking an erroneous decision in rejecting the application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code.</u>

11. We have also perused the ex-parte decree which is as under:

"plff, files hazira. The record is taken up for ex-parte hearing P,W.1) Anil Kumar Banik and P.W,2) Abul Mokaram Chowdhury examined on S.A. Document marked Ext.1 for the plff. The suit is proved C.F. paid is adequate. Hence, it is.

Ordered

That the suit be decreed ex-parte against the defdts without cost. Defdts. No.1/2 are directed to execute and register a kabala for the S/L in favour of the plff, within 40 days from this date i.e. the plff. shall get the same through the Court. The plff. is directed to deposit balance consideration money of Taka..5000/- (five thousand) within 30 days from this date i.e. the order shall stand cancelled."

12. From the order decreeing the suit ex-parte, it is apparent that the Court decreed the suit as a matter of course without coming to any finding whether, in fact, the defendant entered into an agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit land and whether any consideration passed.

13. For the reasons stated hereinbefore, we find substance in the appeal.

14. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed subject to payment of cost of taka 10,000.00 to the plaintiff-respondent. The impugned judgment and order affirming the order of the learned Subordinate Judge is set aside. The application filed under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code is allowed and the ex-parte decree passed in the suit (Title Suit No.137 of 1986) on 25.02.1987 is set aside and the suit is restored to its original file and member. The trial Court is directed to proceed with suit and dispose the same in accordance with law as expeditiously as possible. The parties are directed to maintain status-quo in respect of the possession and the position of the suit land till disposal of the suit. The petitioner is directed to deposit the cost of taka 10,000.00 in the trial Court in the name of the plaintiff within 3(three months from the date of receipt of this judgment failing which this appeal shall stand dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule has been posted in the list for hearing on the prayer of both the sides on maintainability of the same on the application filed by the defendant-opposite party-applicant.

2. The plaintiff-petitioner filed the revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, hereinafter referred as the Code, and obtained the Rule challenging the impugned judgment and decree dated 22-4-2004 passed in Title Suit No. 353/2003 by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Second Court, Dhaka rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code on the application filed by the defendant-opposite party- applicant.

3. Facts of the case, in short, is that the plaintiff-petitioner filed the suit for permanent injunction against the defendant-opposite party-applicant stating, inter alia, that he was a monthly tenant under him in respect of the suit premises under a renewable agreement of tenancy for a period of 2(two) years which expired on 30-4-2003. The plaintiff-petitioner, however, is in possession of the suit premises by holding over by paying rents through the House Rent Controller in House Rent Case No. 25 of 2003 since the defendant-opposite party applicant, who is the landlord, refused to accept the rent tendered and later sent by post by him. The defendant-opposite party having threatened to evict the petitioner forcibly, he brought the suit for permanent injunction.

4. Defendant-opposite party appeared in the suit and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code for rejecting the plaint on the ground that the tenancy agreement with the plaintiff having expired he has no legal character, no locus standi and no cause of action to bring the suit as there is no breach of any obligation or contract.

5. The trial Court allowed the said application on contest rejecting the plaint by the impugned judgment and decree. Hence this Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner.

6. The defendant-opposite party has filed the application for discharging the Rule as not maintain- able on two-fold reasons. Firstly, the judgment and decree rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code being a decree within the meaning of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code is an appealable decree and not revisable one; secondly, the instant revision is not also maintainable either under section 115(1) or under section 115(4) of the Code.

7. Pressing the application, Mr. Sk Md Morshed, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party, submits with reference to the relevant provisions of sub-section (2) of section 2, section 96 and Order XLIII of the Code that the instant Rule is not maintainable. Elaborating his first objection, Mr Morshed submits that the impugned order comes within the meaning of decree as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code. inasmuch as the trial Court passed the impugned decree conclusively determining the right of the parties and secondly, the rejection of the plaint itself is a decree as defined thereunder and the same being an appealable decree under section 96 of the Code, the instant Rule is liable to be discharged as not maintainable. Referring the provision of Order XLIII of the Code, Mr Morshed submits that since the impugned decree is an appealable decree and not included as an appealable order under Order XLIII(1) of the Code no revision lies against the same. Elaborating his second ground of objection, Mr Morshed submits with reference to the provision of sub-sections (1) and (4) of section 115 of the Code that the impugned decree having not been passed by the learned District Judge, Additional District Judge or Joint District Judge, or a decree passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, from which no appeal lies but the impugned decree being an appealable decree passed by Senior Assistant Judge as provided in sub-section (1) of section 115 of the Code nor the impugned decree is an order passed by the District Judge or Additional District Judge under sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 115 of the Code the Rule is liable to be discharged as not maintainable. Mr Morshed has referred a decision in the case of S. Azizul Hassan and another vs Malik Ghulam Muhammad reported in 1971 SCMR 123 in support if his submission.

8. In reply Mr ASM Ramzan Khan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner, filed a counter-affidavit and vehemently opposed the application contending that the application is liable to be rejected. He submits that since the impugned decree is not a decree as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code but only a formal decree the same is neither an appealable decree nor an appeal could be filed against the same under section 96 of the Code except a revision under section 115(1) of the Code, inasmuch as the trial Court rejected his plaint without conclusively determining the rights of the parties. He further submits that since the impugned decree is not in the nature of a decree as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code the same is a revisable one and not an appealable decree and, as such, the application is misconceived and is liable to be rejected. In support of his submission Mr Khan has cited the decisions in the case of Shankar Rao and others vs Raghunathrao, reported in AIR 1926 (Nag) 75(1) and the case of Forman Ali Dewan and another vs Munsur Ali and ors, reported in 13 DLR 836.

9. Mr Khan contends, elaborating his submission, that Order XLIII provides appeal from appealable orders but an order under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code has not been included in the same for filing a Miscellaneous Appeal. So, no appeal lies against the impugned order rejecting the plaint. He also elaborates that the impugned judgment and decree though included in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code is a formal decree not in the nature of the definition of a decree given there since the impugned decree does not contain all the characteristics of a decree defined therein. Hence, no appeal lies against the same under section 96 or under the provisions of Order XLIII of the Code. Mr. Khan further submits that the plaintiff-petitioner filed the suit for permanent injunction and the defendant-opposite party filed the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code soon after his appearance in the suit for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the plaintiff has no legal right, locus standi, cause of action, etc. and the trial Court upon hearing the parties rejected the plaint by the impugned judgment and decree without framing any issue, taking any evidence and conclusively determining the rights of the plaintiff to sue. He concludes contending that therefore the present revision is maintainable.

10. In reply Mr Sk Md Morshed, tile learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, submits that the provision laid down in Order VII, rule 11 of the Code is a summary procedure giving the Court power to reject a plain reading of the same and there is no necessity of framing any issue or taking any evidence in rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code.

11. Perused the application, the counter- affidavit and heard the learned Advocates of both the sides.

12. The applicant was the defendant in the suit brought by the plaintiff-petitioner for permanent injunction against him restraining him from evicting them from the suit premises. The defendant- applicant filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code before the trial Court for rejection of the plaint on the ground that since the tenancy agreement has expired the plaintiff has had no legal character, locus standi, cause of action, etc. for filing the suit. The trial Court, on perusal of the application and the plaint and on hearing the parties, rejected the plaint allowing the application holding that "We see the plaintiff has no legal character or locus standi to come with this suit as his tenancy right has already been exhausted."

13. In order to dispose of the application addressing the submissions of the learned Advocates of both the sides it is necessary to quote the relevant provisions of the sections and Order of the Code referred by them.

Sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code is as follows:

"(2) "decree" means the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final. It shall be deemed to include the rejection of a plaint and the determination of any question within .......... section 144 but shall not include-

(a) any adjudication from which an appeal lies as an appeal from an order, or

(b) any order of dismissal for default.

Explanation-A decree is preliminary when further proceedings have to be taken before the suit can be completely disposed of. It is final when such adjudication completely disposes of the suit. It may be partly preliminary and partly final".

Section 96 of the Code runs as follows:

"96(1) Save where otherwise expressly provided in the body of this Code or by any other law for the time being in force, an appeal shall lie from every decree passed by any Court exercising original jurisdiction to the Court authorised to hear appeals, from the decisions of such Court.

(2) An appeal may lie from an original decree passed ex parte.

(3) No appeal shall lie from a decree passed by the Court without the consent of parties.

Section 115(1) provides as follows:

115(1) The High Court Division may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the records of any suit or proceeding, in which a decree or an order has been passed by a Court of District Judge, or Additional District Judge, or a decree has been passed by a court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge, from which no appeal lies: and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such decree or order occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division may revise such decree or order and, make such order in the suit or proceeding. as it thinks fit.

(2) The Court of District Judge may, on the application of any party aggrieved, call for the record of any suit or proceeding, in which an order has been passed by a Court of Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies; and if such Court appears to have committed any error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of justice, the Court of District Judge may revise such order and make such order as it thinks fit.

(3) A Court of Additional District Judge shall have all the powers of the District Judge under sub-section (2) in respect of revision case which may be transferred to it by the District Judge.

(4) An application to the High Court Division for revision of an order of the District Judge or Additional District Judge as the case may be, made under sub-sections (2) or (3) shall lie, where the High Court Division grants leave for revision on an error of an important question of law resulting in erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice, and the High Court Division may make such order in the suit or proceeding as it thinks fit."

14. We also need to examine the provision of Order VII, rule 11 of the Code which runs as follows:

"11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action:

(b) where the relief claimed is under-valued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so:

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so:

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."

The impugned order being a decree and not an appealable order provisions of Order XLIII of the Code have no application.

15. While disposing the application on the maintainability of the Rule this court is not obliged to give any finding on the merit of impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court. The question that arose before this Court on the application is to see whether the Rule is maintainable on the grounds taken in the application filed by the defendant-opposite party-appellant.

16. The objections to the maintainability of the Rule has been made on two grounds, whether the impugned decree amounts to a decree as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code is an appealable decree and no revision lies. The second objection is that the instant Rule issued on the revisional application filed under section 115(1) of the Code is not maintainable against the impugned judgment and decree.

17. On the other hand, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner contends that the revision is maintainable against the impugned judgment and decree because the same is not a decree in the nature of a decree as defined in sub- section (2) of section 2 of the Code, since there has been no conclusive determination of the rights of the parties, the decree drawn up is a formal decree and does not contain the characteristic of a decree defined thereunder, etc. In the case between Shanker Rao and others vs Raghunath Rao, reported in AIR 1926 (Nagpur) 75(1) cited by Mr Khan in support of his submission it was held-

"The mere drawing up of a formal decree does not ipso Jac to make the corresponding order an appealable one, if it does not, in itself, really fall within the definition of a decree."

He also referred another decision in the case of Forman Ali Dewan and another vs Munsur Ali and ors, reported in 13 DLR 836, where it has been laid down that-

"It has been held that rejection of a plaint is not a decree in all cases, but if the rejection of plaint goes so far as to determine the question between the parties, then it will operate as a decree."

<u>18. In view of the above, let me now quote and examine the finding of the impugned judgment. In disposing of the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code rejecting the plaint, the learned Senior Assistant Judge has clearly held that "the plaintiff has no legal character or locus standi to come with this suit as his tenancy right has already been exhausted." A decree means as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code as "the formal expression of an adjudication which, so far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may be either preliminary or final." In the instant impugned judgment, the learned Senior Assistant Judge rejected the plaint clearly finding that the plaintiff has no legal character or locus standi to come with this Suit as his tenancy right has already been exhausted which has conclusively determined the right of the plaintiff to sue. The provision of sub- section (2) of section 2 of the Code also includes a decree on rejecting of a plaint. It appears from the facts that the impugned decree rejecting, the plaint has been passed under clause (a) of rule 11. This is a settled principle that a court can reject a plaint under clause (a) on a plain reading of the same. The trial Court has rejected the plaint following clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code giving his reasons and findings determining the rights of the parties and, as such, the same .is a decree as defined in sub-section (2) of the Code. The trial Court rejected the plaint on the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code exercising its power vested therein. This is a special and summary procedure empowering the Court to reject the plaint for 4(four) reasons as quoted above. The Court has rejected the plaint exercising its power given in clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code. This is not disputed that Court may reject the plaint under clause (a) on a plain reading of the plaint itself without framing any issue and taking any evidence. When the objection- ground taken under rule 11 is surfaced from plain reading of the plaint from the facts not disputed, the Court can reject the plaint in summary procedure. But whether the Court has exercised its power properly or not or whether the Court has erred in law in rejecting the plaint under rule 11 of Order VII of the Code without framing issue and taking evidence is not before me to give a decision while disposing this application. I, therefore, find no substance in the submission of Mr Khan, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, that the impugned decree does not have the characteristic of a decree as defined in sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Code as the trial Court did not determine the rights of the party conclusively by taking evidence on the issue framed. I also do not find the decisions referred by him have any application in the instant case since the trial Court has conclusively determined the right of the parties. The impugned decree is very much a proper decree and not mere a formal decree which is an appealable decree under section 96 of the Code. In that view of the matter, I find substance in the submission of Mr Sk Md Morshed, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party-applicant. The decision reported in 1971 SCMR 123, cited by him as mentioned above clearly laid down that "the trend of judicial opinion is now to the effect that if a decree or an order, which is in the nature of a decree under the Code of Civil Procedure, has been passed by the Court of first instance, and it is appealable under the Code, then whether the appeal lies immediately to the High Court or only after another appeal has been taken before the District Judge, the revision would not be competent." It clearly expressed the view that a decree passed by a Court of first instance is appealable and not revisable. In agreement with the same I am of the opinion that the instant civil revision is not maintainable.</u>

19. Regarding second objection against the maintainability of the Rule as urged by Mr Morshed that the instant revision also does not lie under the provision of sub-section (1) of section 115 of the Code since impugned decree is an appealable decree passed by a court of first instance of a Senior Assistant Judge. He also argued that the impugned decree having not been passed by the learned District Judge or Additional District Judge under sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 115 of the Code the instant Rule is liable to be discharged as not maintainable.

<u>20. Admittedly, the revision has been taken against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge under sub-section (1) of section 115 of the Code. On examining the provision of section 115 of the Code I am of the opinion, agreeing with the submission of Mr. Morshed, that the instant impugned decree having been passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge of the first instance which is appealable as already found by me, the instant civil revision does not lie. Provision of sub-section (1) of section 115 of the Code can only be invoked against an order or decree passed by the learned District Judge or Additional District Judge or against the decree passed by the Joint District Judge, Senior Assistant Judge or Assistant Judge from which no appeal lies. The impugned decree having also not been passed by the learned District Judge or Additional District Judge no revision lies under sub-section (4) of section 115 of the Code, the present Civil revision is misconceived.</u>

21. In view of the above, the Rule is liable to be discharged as not maintainable. In consideration of my above finding I find merit in the application. In the result, the application is allowed.

22. The Rule is discharged as not maintainable without any order as to costs.

23. The order passed earlier calling for the records of the case by this Court is hereby recalled and the order of status quo granted earlier by this court is also vacated.

Send down the lower court records at once if already received by the office of this Court.

End.
