full_judgment:
ATM Fazle Kabir J: This appeal, at the instance of defendant-appellants is preferred against the judgment and decree dated 24-10-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 1219 of 1985 decreeing the suit for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendants from the suit property.

2. The short facts relevant for the purpose of the appeal are that the plaintiff-respondent brought the original suit for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession and realisation of mesne profits. The case of plaintiff-respondent. in short, is that the lands described in the schedule 'A' and 'B' originally belonged to the owners of the Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Bhowal Raj Courts of Wards Estate who donated the same along with some other lands to their family deity Sri Sri Madhab shortly after CS operation. That Bhowal Raj Estate including the debuttar properties were being managed by the Courts of Wards and accordingly, the Manager of the said Estate had been possessing the said proportion by letting out the same to Adhi Bargadars. While the property described in the schedule 'A' and 'B' was under management of the Court of Wards, then the defendant No.1 Md Chand Mia took settlement of suit land as Adhi Bargader by executing a registered Barga rabulyat purported to be lease for 10 years with effect from 1371 BS. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 198 of 1971 and Title Suit No. 226 of 1971 against the defendant Chand Mia for recovery of khas possession in respect of the properties described in the schedule A and realisation of mesne profits for the property described in the schedule B. These two suits were transferred to the Subordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka for disposal and were renumbered as Title Suit No. 14 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 respectively. That the defendant No.1 Chand Mia made appearance in the suit but did not contest in the long run and subsequently the said suits were disposed of and decreed on 26-11-1976 and 24-2-1977 respectively. The defendant No. 1 Chand Mia brought two Miscellaneous cases being Nos. 44 of 1976 and 10 of 1977 to set aside the decrees passed in Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 14 of 1976, but ultimately those two cases were dismissed on 20-8-1977 and 16-7-1977 respectively. Thereafter, the plaintiff respondent filed Execution Case No. 2 of 1977 and Execution Case No. 7 of 1977 for recovery of khas possession and in due course the plaintiff-respondent got recovery of khas possession over the suit property, in due process of law by removing the structures therefrom with the help of police. That one Asraf Ali brought Title Suit No. 31 of 1979, but that Asraf Ali, Kanchan Mia and others took lease of the same plots from the Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate for the period of last four months of 1384 BS. The plaintiff has been in possession of the suit properties through Adhi Bargaders. The defendant Nos. 1 and 3 took lease of the suit land described in schedule-A and B by executing two kabulyats for the year of 1386 BS only but they continued their illegal possession even after expiry of their lease period. The defendant No. 1 along with the vendors of the defendant Nos. 2, 4, 5 and 6 have not given up their illegal possession and they finally refused to give up possession of the property on 11-7-1979. Hence the suit is for recovery of khas possession by evicting the defendants therefrom.

That the defendant Nos. 2-4,5,6 and 7 contested the original suit by filing separate written statements. The case of the defendant No. 6 A. Hai in short, is that the suit property originally belonged to Chand Mia and Bashiruddin in equal share and their names were duly recorded in SA Khatian No. 63 in respect of the suit land. While Chand Mia was in possession of the suit property he sold 1.05 acres of land of plat No. 147 to the defendant No.6 A Hai by a registered kabala deed dated 20-6-1976. It is further stated that the suit property never belonged to Sree Sree Modhob and no deed of endorsement was made by the Bhowal Raj Estate. That the defendant No.1 Chand Mia never executed a kabulyat in favour of the Bhowal Raj Estate as its Adhi Bargadar rather, he took settlement of the suit land from the ex-landlords in whose names CS Khatian No. 7 was prepared. That Sri Sri Madhob the Deity of Hindu Community did not acquire any title in respect of the suit land, but the employees of the Bhowal Raj Esstate have created some forged documents in order to grab the property of the defendants as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

The learned Subordinate Judge after perusing the plaint and written statement framed issues for determination of the real controversy between the parties. Both the parties examined their respective witnesses and upon considering the evidences available on record the learned Subordinate Judge decree the suit by the impugned judgment dated 24-10-1996.

3. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied by the impugned judgment and decree the defendant appellant preferred this appeal stating that the trial Court committed an error in decreeing the original suit.

4. Mr Matiur Rahman, the learned Advocate appears on behalf of the appellants while Mr Md Abdul Haque and Mr Debdas Samaddar, the learned Advocates appear on behalf of the respondents to resist the appeal.

5. Mr ABM Motiur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant appellants, submits that the alleged kabulyat executed by the defendant Chand Mia is a forged and fabricated document but the learned Subordinate Judge wrongly treated it as genuine. The learned Advocate further submits that the PW 2 admitted in his cross-examination that they took delivery of possession of the suit land by paper transaction but, in fact, they could not recover the suit land. The learned Advocate then submits that the witnesses of the plaintiff have failed to prove his case in spite of the fact the learned Subordinate Judge most illegally decreed the suit by the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate further submits that the suit land was duly recorded in SA Khatian No. 63 in the names of Chand Mia and Bashruddin who are the vendors of the defendant appellant No.6 has proved their possession in the suit land, but the learned Subordinate Judge failed to appreciate the evidenciary value of such documents relating to records of right. The learned Advocate incidentally submits that the scheduled land of the plaint does not tally with the documents relating to alleged gift in the name of the deity made by the plaintiff respondent. It is contended that in the absence of specific land no decree for recovery of possession can be granted, but the learned Subordinate Judge most illegally decreed the suit without considering practical aspect of the law. The learned Advocate cited several rulings reported in 4 DLR 447, 7 DLR 61 and 12 DLR 246 and by referring these decisions the learned Advocate submits that under BT Act oral settlement was permissible, as such there was no necessity of document to create tenancy. In view of the fact defendant Chand Mia, the vendor of the appellant took oral settlement from the original landlord, but the learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider the legal aspect of such oral settlement.

6. Mr Md Abdul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent, submits that it is an admitted fact that the suit property originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate and it is also undisputed that CS Khatian No.7 was recorded in respect of properties including the suit land in the name of superior landlords of the Bhowel Raj Estate. The learned Advocate then submits that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Court of Wards in SA and RS Khatians. (Exhibits-4 & 4 ka) in the name of Sree Sree Mahdhob and the plaintiff paid rents to the government in respect of the suit land. The learned Advocate incidentally submits that Chand Mia, the vender of the defendant No.6, executed a registered kabulyat as Adhi Bargadar under the plaintiff in the year 1371 BS, as such, the defendant No.6 and his vendor Chand Mia acquired no right, title and interest in the suit property. The learned Advocate further submits that the plaintiff-respondent got the decree in Title Suit No. 12 of 1976 and Title Suit No. 14 of 1976 and they took delivery of possession in the suit property by filing Execution case in due process of law, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly decreed the suit by the impugned judgment. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendant No.6 new appellant No. 1 Abdul Hye has claimed 1.05 acres of land, but no document was produced and examined by the defendant in support of his claim in the Court below, as such, this appeal has no substance to interfere in the impugned judgment and accordingly the appeal is liable to be dismissed how lot us examine the evidence on record for its critical analysis.

7. It appears from the record that the plaintiff respondent examined 2 witnesses while the defendant-appellants examined 2 witnesses in the Court below.

8. PW 1 Lehaz Uddin Prodhan is the Head Assistant of the Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate, who stated that the suit property originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate and it was donated to Sree Sree Madhob, the Deity of the Bhowal Raj Estate. It is further stated that the defendant Chand Mia took Adhi Barga of the suit land from the plaintiff-respondent by executing a register Kabulyat in 1371 BS. Thereafter, the plaintiff brought two Title suits against Chand Mia and obtained decree for recovery of possession in the suit land. He denied the suggestion that Chand Mia never executed kabulyat in favour of the Court of Wards.

9. PW 2 SMA Kadir is the Assistant Chief Manager of Bhowal Raj Estate, who corroborated the plaintiff's case to the effect that the suit property was duly recorded in the name of the Deity Sri Sri Madhob both in SA and RS Khatians, and the vendor of the defendant-appellant named Chand Mia took settlement some portion of the suit land by executing registered kabulyats on 1-8-1963 (Exhibit-1 series) in favour of Bhowal Raj Estate. In cross, he says that after the abolition of Jamindari in 1950 the government acquired the properties of Bhowal Raj Estate save and except the choiced land and debutter land. He further stated in cross that the vendor of the appellant Chand Mia took Adhi-Barga of the suit land in 1371 BS for ten years and subsequently he was evicted from the suit land through process of law in pursuance of the Execution case. He further stated that they got recovery of possession through paper transaction but, in fact, could not got real possession of the property. On the other hand, the defendant side examined two witnesses. DW 1 Zobed Ali has stated that the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate from whom Chand Mia and Bashir Uddin took Pattan of the suit land and it was recorded in the names of Chand Mia, and Bashir Uddin in SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit ka-1). He denied the suggestion that Chand Mia took Barga by executing barga-kabulyat in favour of the Bhowal Raj Estate. But in cross, he says that Chand Mia took Adhi-Barga of the suit land by executing a kubilyat dated 1-8-1963 in favour of Bhowal Raj Estate and he purchased 1.05 acres of land from that Chand Mia. He further says that he cannot say whether the Bhowal Raj Estate obtained a decree for recovery of khas possession by evicting Chand Mia from the suit land. DW 2 Md Khadem Hossain, the Manager of the Court of Wards of the Bhowal Raj Estate, deposed but did not give any material evidence in this case.

<u>10. On careful scrutiny of the evidence, of both oral and documentary, it is an admitted fact that the suit property originally belonged to ex-landlord of Bhowal Raj Estate and CS Khatian No.7 was duly prepared in their names including the suit property. There is no denying that the property of Bhowal Raj Estate is now being managed and controlled by the Court or wards in respect of choiced land and debutter properties of Bhowal Raj Estate. It is the definite case of the plaintiff than Chand Mia, the vendor of the defendant No.6, executed a registered kubilyat in favour of Court of Wards of Bhowal Raj Estate in 1371 BS Exhibit 1 is the registered kabilyat dated 1-8-1963 executed by the defendant Chand Mia, which shows that he took Adhi barga in respect of the land of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab from the plaintiff for the period of 10 years including the suit plot No. 147. It appears from the said kabilyat that the suit land belonged to the Deity Sree Sree Madhab under Bhowal Raj Estate managed by the Court of Wards. If we consider the cases of both the defendant appellants as well as the plaintiff-respondent side by side, we find that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate. It is also undisputed that the property of Bhowal Raj Estate is being managed and controlled by the Court of Wards. It appears from the registered kabilyat dated 1-8-1963 (Exhibit 1) that the defendant Chand Mia executed the deed for taking Adhi-Barga in respect of the debuttor land belonging to the Deity Sree Sree Madhab under management of the Court of Wards. The defendant-appellant has examined only two witnesses who have tried to say that the kabulyat (Exhibit 1) executed by Chand Mia was never acted upon but it appears from the recitals of the said Kubilyat that the defendant Chand Mia admitted that suit land was debutter property of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab. According to the provision of section 92 of the Evidence Act, the oral evidence is always excluded by the documentary evidence and the oral evidence cannot invalidate the contents of the document unless it is proved to be product of forgery. In the instant case, we find that the plaintiff-respondent filed certified copies of both SA Khatian No. 63 and RS Khatian No. 506 (Exhibit Nos. 4, 4ka) in the Court below in 1973 which show that the suit land was recorded in the name of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab Bigroho and others. On the other hand, the defendant-appellant also filed a certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 in respect of the same land showing recorded in the name of the defendant Chand Mia. It appears that the defendant-appellant obtained certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 in the year of 1991. Under such circumstances the learned trial Court should have called for the original Khatian volume in order to compare and find out the genuine one, but the trial Court failed to do so.</u>

11. We have perused both the certified copies of SA Khatian No. 63 in respect of the same land. It appears that the defendant appellant obtained certified copy of the SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit- Ka-1) which shows that the Record Room prepared it and the comparing clerk compared the certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 on 28-10-1986 but it is curious enough that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued the said certified copy by putting his signature on 15-3-1991. i.e. after the lapse of about 5 years from the date of its preparation. Such inordinate delay without explanation in obtaining the alleged certified copy of SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit-Ka-1) gives sufficient indications to hold that it is the product of collusion and forgery for the purpose of this suit.

12. In view of the fact, we are of opinion that the certified copy of the SA Khatian No. 63 (Exhibit Ka-1) in respect of the suit land filed by the plaintiff-respondent appears to be genuine one, which was recorded in the names of the Deity Sree Sree Madhab and original landlords. In view of the fact, we are inclined to hold that plaintiff is still absolute owner of the property on the basis of evidence on record. It is also an admitted fact that the suit land originally belonged to Bhowal Raj Estate managed and controlled by the Court of Wards. It further appears from the certified copy of the decree 14 of 1976 (Exhibit-2) that the plaintiff in the earlier occasion filed a suit for recovery of possession against defendant Chand Mia in respect of suit plot No. 147 and obtained decree. It in further evident in the record that Chand Mia defendant No. 1 filed Miscellaneous case for setting aside the decree of that suit, but it was dismissed. So it is proved from the documentary evidence that the decree of Title Suit No. 14 of 1977 is still binding upon the defendant No. 1 Chand Mia from whom the defendant-appellants allegedly purchased some portion of the suit land subsequent to the decree passed in Title Suit No. 14 of 1976. It is further revealed from the certified copy of the report (Exhibit-gha) of process server dated 2-2-1978 that the process server Shahjahan Gazi handed over the possession of the suit land of plot No. 147 to the plaintiff-respondent in Execution Case No. 7 of 1977. It is evident from the documentary evidences on record that the plaintiff-respondent obtained symbolic possession over the suit property on 2-2-1978 and he filed the instant suit for recovery of khas possession in the year of 1985 within 12 years from date of taking delivery of possession through Court, as such the question of adverse possession claimed by the defendant-appellants does not arise.

13. It is a settled principle of law in the civil matter when a party asserts a positive fact who should be called upon to prove his assertion and not the party who denies the fact. In the instant case, defendant-appellants want the Court to believe that they purchased suit land by deeds from the vendor Chand Mia, who took settlement of the same from Bhowal Raj Estate, but no oral or documentary evidence has been produced to prove such, settlement of land and subsequent purchase by the appellants.

14. Considering all facts on the record we are constrained to hold that there is no substance to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree, as such this appeal is liable to be dismissed.

15. In the result, the appeal is dismissed but without any order as to costs.

16. The impugned judgment and decree dated 24-10-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur in Title Suit No. 1219 of 1985 is hereby confirmed.

Send down the lower Court records along with a copy of judgment for information and necessary action.

End.

full_judgment:
The judgment-debtors obtained the present Rule from a judgment and order dated 13-6-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Civil Revision No. 15 of 2004 rejecting the revisional application and thereby affirming those of dated 11-1-2004 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Chandanaish, Chittagong, in other Execution case No. 5 of 2002 making an order of arrest of the judgment-debtor for detention in Civil prison for a period of 6(six) weeks.

2. Short facts leading to the issuance of the instant Rule are as follows:

The decree holder opposite party No. 1 has been serving as a Teacher of Bengali Department of Barman Islamia Senior Madrasha since October, 1987. The Governing Body of the Madrasha dismissed him from service on 8-10-1989 and, there- after the decree holder opposite party as plaintiff instituted other Class Suit No. 62 of 1989 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chandanaish, Chittagongfor declaration that the order of dismissal dated 8-10-1989 is illegal. The said suit was decree on contest, against which some of the proceeding of the present petitioners preferred other Appeal No. 203 of 1992 before the District Judge, Chittagong and the said appeal was also dismissed on contest by the judgment and decree dated 12-3-1996. Since the said judgment and decree being not executable, the decree holder opposite party again instituted other Suit No. 10 of 2000 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chandanaish under section 55 of the Specific Relief Act for mandatory injunction to reinstate the decree holder opposite party in his position and the said suit was decreed by the judgment and decree on 9-10-2001 and the Madrasha Authority was directed to reinstate the decree holder opposite party in his post. Subsequently the decree holder opposite party instituted other Execution case No.5 of 2002 and the present judgment-debtor petitioners were asked to appear personally in the Court and to submit reply as to why allegations for contempt/violation of the Court should not be brought against them. The present judgment-debtor petitioners appeared in the Court and prayed for time to give reply to the show cause notice and on 8-6-2003 judgment-debtor petitioners filed an application before the Executing Court stating, inter alia, that they were ready to allow the decree holder opposite party to join in his post and they further stated that the decree holder did not go to Madrasha to join on 7-6-2003.

3. The learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 11-1-2004 directed the decree holder opposite party to pay amounting to Taka 100 as cost of Civil imprisonment for each judgment-debtor as per Order XXI, Rule 39(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and also passed an order of arrest against the judgment-debtor petitioners to put them in Civil prison for a period of 6 (six) weeks under section 58 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4. Being aggrieved by the said order the judgment-debtor petitioners preferred Civil Revision No. 15 of 2004 before the learned District Judge, Chittagong and eventually the said revision was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong, who by the impugned judgment and order dated 13-6-2004 rejected the revisional application and affirmed the order passed by the Executing Court.

5. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order, the judgment obtained the present rule by filling the present revisional application.

6. Mr Fariduddin Khan, the learned Advocates for the petitioners submits that the trial Court passed the order of Civil imprisonment without following the procedure as laid down under Order XXI, rule 32(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned Additional District Judge without considering the said aspect upheld the said order and as such committed error of law in arriving its decision. He further submits that by filing application the judgment-debtors intimated the learned Executing Court that they were fully respectful and obedient to the Court's judgment and order and they issued letter to the decree holder opposite party to join in his post but the decree holder did not join his post by raising some unnecessary and irrational reasons.

7. On the other hand Mrs Farida Khan, the learned Advocate of the decree holder opposite party submits that in passing the impugned order the Courts below did not commit any error or irregularity as the judgment-debtors willfully disobeyed the Court's order. However she frankly conceded that before passing the order of imprisonment, the trial Court should have given a change of hearing to the judgment-debtors. I appreciate this submission of the learned Advocate of the decree-holder-opposite party.

8. Heard the learned Advocate, perused the revisional application, the impugned judgment and orders and the records. From the order dated 11-1- 2004 passed by the learned Assistant Judge it appears that in passing the order of civil imprisonment, in fact the Court did neither assign any reason whatsoever, nor he expressed what satisfaction he had in passing the order of civil imprisonment. The' learned Assistant Judge simply quoted the provision of section 58 and orders 21 rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure and passed the order. The learned Additional District Judge in passing the impugned judgment and order held that the executing Court rightly proceeded as per provision of Order XXI, rule 32(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. Mr Fariduddin Khan the learned Advocate for the petitioners raised a question that the Executing Court should have started a miscellaneous case to ascertain whether the judgment-debtors violated the Court's order. In reply to that Mrs Farida Khan submits that in Order XXI, rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure there is no such provision.

10. It is true that, in Order XXI, rule 32(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, there is no provision for directing an enquiry to see the truthness or otherwise of the allegations of willful disobedience or violation of a decree for permanent or mandatory injunction. But the question is how a Court can take action against the alleged delinquent without any proof of the alleged violation without making an inquiry into the matter to satisfy itself about the allegations against the defaulting judgment-debtor.

11. In the instant case from the records it appears that in the execution proceeding when the Court asked the present petitioners to appear before it, the petitioners personally had appeared before the Court and by filing application on 7-6-2003 they stated that they did not disobey the Court's order. Since the members of the previous committee were not available, after getting notice from the Court the members of the present managing committee have taken step to reinstate the decree holder in his post. By filing another application on 8-6-2003 the present petitioners also informed the executing Court that when the Court directed the judgment-debtors petitioners to reinstate the decree holder in his post, the judgment-debtors petitioners asked the decree holder to join his post and give a letter of joining. But ultimately he did not join his post. When the judgment-debtors appeared in the Court and by filing application had stated the above facts that, they asked the holder opposite party to join his post and the decree holder did not join to his post on this or that plea, the Executing Court ought to have made an enquiry whether the above assertions of the judgment-debtors were true or false, before passing the order of Civil imprisonment. I am of the view that in not holding such inquiry, the Executing Court committed an error of law and the learned Additional District Judge also committed illegality in affirming the said order of the Executing Court.

<u>12. Before taking any action under Order XXI, rule 32 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the delinquent the Court must be satisfied that the judgment-debtor has willfully disobeyed or violated the Court's order of injunction. An enquiry on the allegations of wilful disobedience or violation of injunction by the judgment-debtors is therefore essential before taking any positive action against the delinquent. The Court shall not act mechanically and blindly to punish a judgment-debtor without affording him any opportunity of being heard. Further a Court of law cannot punish anybody with- out being satisfied to the effect that the judgment- debtor has wilfully disobeyed or violated the decree/ order of injunction. We find support of the above view in the case of Jiban Bima Corporation vs Mahibul Majid, reported in 52 DLR 186.</u>

13. Having discussed above, I find merit in the Rule.

14. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Chitiagong in Civil Revision No. 15 of 2004 affirming the order dated 11-1-2004 passed by the learned Sessions Judge, Chandanaish, Chittagong in other Execution case No.5 of 2002 is hereby set aside. However, the Executing Court is directed to make an inquiry as to whether there has been a wilful disobedience or violation of the decree of mandatory injunction by the judgment-debtors and to dispose of the execution case within 4 (four) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and order.

15. The order of stay passed at the time of the issuance of the rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
FRM Nazmul Ahasan J : This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and order dated 25-3-2008 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Sylhet in Civil Revision No.79 of 2005 dismissing the Civil Revision and thereby affirming the Judgment and Order dated 20-7-2005 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet in Title Suit No.120 of 2004 Rejecting an application filed by the defendant-petitioners under Order 7 rule 11 read with sections 11 and 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set-aside.

2. The relevant facts of this case are that the present opposite party as plaintiff instituted the Title Suit No.120 of 2004 impleading the petitioners as defendants in the Court of Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet praying for declaration that the Kabala dated 15-7-2004 in favour of defendant Nos.1-5 executed by the defendant No.6 and the kabala dated 22-4-2004 executed by defendant Nos.7-9 in favour of defendant No.6 and the Judgment and decree dated 21-12-1988 passed in Title Suit No.68 of 1984 and the Judgment and decree dated 1-4-1996 in Title Appeal No. 60 of 1989 being obtained by practicing fraud which are not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. On 10-3-2005 the defendant Nos.I-5 and the defendant Nos.6-9 filed two separate applications for rejection of plaintiff under Order 7 rule II read section 11 and section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendant's case, in short, is that the father of the defendant Nos.7-9 Anil Ranjan Shyam filed Title Suit No.68 of 1984 praying for declaration that the suit property was not enemy property and the Enemy Case No.58 of 1966-67 was illegal that the said suit was decreed and thereupon, the Government filed Title Appeal No. 60 of 1989 and the appeal was dismissed on contest on 1-4-1996 and thereafter, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (revenue) filed a Civil Revision No. 2836 of 1999 before this Court and on 20-6-1999, the same was summarily rejected on the ground that the application was barred by limitation; that the plaintiff did not take any step against the order of rejection; that Anil Ranjan Shyam then mutated the suit property and a separate Khatian was created in the name of defendant Nos.7-9 and they gifted the said land to the defendant No.6 by the registered deed dated 22-4-2004 and the defendant No.6 got the same mutated in his name, created a separate Khatian and then sold the same to the defendant Nos.1-5 by registered deed and since then the defendant Nos. 1-5 are owning and possessing the suit land; that on 3-8-2004 the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Sylhet cancelled the mutation created in the name of the defendant No.6 and passed an order to vacate the land within 7 days without serving any notice and without giving any opportunity of being heard and while the defendant No.6 and defendant Nos.1-5 came to know about the matter, they filed two separate Writ Petitions being Writ Petition No.4646 of 2004 and 4443 of 2004 before this Court and obtained Rule and the operation of the memo of cancellation and vacating the suit land was stayed and the Writ Petitions are still pending before this Court; that the plaintiff filed the suit by concealing the facts regarding the Civil Revision and Writ Petition and the suit is barred by res-judicata, barred by limitation and is liable to be rejected.

4. The plaintiff contested the application by filing a written objection against it stating, inter alia, that the defendants filed this application only to delay the disposal of the suit and to harass the plaintiff and, as such, the application is liable to be rejected. Upon hearing the parties the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Sylhet rejected the aid application on 20-7-2005.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid order passed by the learned Joint District Judge, the defendant-petitioners filed Civil Revision No.79 of 2005 before the Court of District Judge. The learned Additional District Judge upon hearing the Civil Revision rejected the same by his Judgment and order-dated 25-3-2008.

6. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Judgment and order defendant-petitioners preferred Revisional application under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. Mr Tabarak Hussain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has filed a supplementary affidavit dated 3-5-2011 annexing the Judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No.68 of 1984 and Judgment and decree dated 1-4-1996 passed by the Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Sylhet in Title Appeal No.60 of 1989.

8. On the other hand, learned Deputy Attorney General has filed counter affidavit dated 10-5-2011.

9. Mr Tabarak Hussain; the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned Additional District Judge upon gross misconception of law and facts disallowed the Civil Revision which resulted in an error occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that both the Courts below failed to appreciate that the present suit is barred by limitation and it appears from paragraph Nos.5 and 6 of the plaint that the subject matter of the present suit and the earlier suit was similar and both the Courts Below failed to consider that the suit is barred by res-judicata and, as such, Courts below committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice.

10.Mr Goutam Kumar Roy, the learned Deputy Attorney General after supporting the Judgment of the Courts below submits that there was a long delay of 822 days in filing this Revisional application and there was no separate application for condonation of delay in which the delay is explained properly and thus the Rule may be discharged on the ground of limitation. He further submits that the present suit was filed praying that the alleged kabala was a created and forged one and the Judgment and decree of the Courts below obtained upon practicing fraud and there is specific cause of action in the suit which cannot be rejected in a summary manner upon an application by the defendant-petitioners without framing issues and taking evidence in the suit.

11. We have heard the learned Advocate of both the sides and perused the plaint, Judgment and orders of the Courts below, Revisional application, the supplementary affidavit and counter affidavit filed by the respective parties.

12. It appears from the order of the trial Court that upon hearing the application preferred by the defendant petitioners, rejected the same with the finding that the question raised in the application are mostly decidable during trial and the question may be enunciated in the issues.

13. The learned Additional District Judge upon discussing the point of limitation as well as the matter raised by the defendant-petitioners on res-judicata properly found that the question of res-judicata is also a question which can be disposed of by framing issues in the suit. So, the rejection of plaint on the ground of limitation and res-judicata should not be allowed merely on the prayer by the defendants side.

14. Mr Tabarak Hussain, the learned Advocate submits that the plaint should have been rejected by the trial Court on the findings that case is barred by the rule of res-judicata. He further submits that it appears from the reading of the paragraph Nos. 5 and 6 of the plaint that the facts and issues in this suit are directly and substantially are issue in the former suit; the present suit is not maintainable on the principle of res-judicata. In support of his submission he referred decision reported in 10 MLR (AD) 144, 10 MLR 344 and 61 DLR 503.

15. In order to appreciate to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, let us examine the contents of the plaint of Title Suit No. 102 of 2004. It appears from the plaint that the plaintiff prayed for the following reliefs-

“অতএব বাদি প্রার্থনা করেন যে,

(ক) ১-৫নং বিবাদী নামীয় ৬নং বিবাদী সম্পাদিত বিগত ১৫-৭-০৪ ইংরেজী তারিখের ১১৯৫৮/০৪ ইং নং রেজিস্টারী সাফ কবলা পন্ড, অকর্মন্য, প্রবৃত্তিহীন, বেআইনী, ফলবলহীন ও অত্র বাদিও উপর তাহা বাধ্যকর ও কার্য্যকরী নহে মর্মে ঘোষণামুলক ডিক্রি দানে।

(খ) ৬নং বিবাদী বরাবরে ৭-৯নং বিবাদী সম্পাদিত বিগত ২২-০৪-০৪ ইংরেজী তারিখের ৬৭৯৯/০৪ ইং নং রেজিষ্টারী দানপত্র পন্ড, অকর্মন্য, প্রাবঞ্চিক, এখতিয়ার বর্হিভূত, বেআইনী, ফলবলহীন ও অত্র বাদিও উপর তাহা বাধ্যকর ও কার্য্যকরী নহে মর্মে ঘোষণামূলক ডিক্রি দানে।

(গ) অত্র ৭-৯ নং বিবাদীর পূর্ববর্তী অনিল রঞ্জন শ্যাম কর্তৃক অত্র বাদি গং বিরুদ্ধে মাননীয় তৎকালীন সাব জজ, ২য় আদালত, সিলেট এ দায়েরী স্বত্ব ৬৮/৮৪ ইং নং মামলায় যথাক্রমে বিগত ২১-১২-৮৮ ইং ও ২৭-১২-৮৮ইং তারিখের রায় ও ডিক্রি এবং তৎ উদভূত স্বত্ব আপীল ৬০/৮৯ ইং মামলায় মাননীয় অতিঃ জেলা জজ, ১ম আদালত, সিলেট কর্তৃক বিগত ০১-০৪-৯৬ ইংরেজী ও বিগত ০৭-০৪-৯৬ ইংরেজী তারিখে প্রদত্ত রায় ও ডিক্রি প্রতারনার আশ্রয়ে হাসিলকৃত গণ্যে তাহা অত্র বাদিও উপর বাধ্যকর ও কার্য্যকরী নহে মর্মে ঘোষণামূলক ডিক্রি দানে।”

16. 'It appears from the Revisional application as well as the supplementary affidavit that the petitioner did not produce the plaint of the earlier suit, through they have submitted the Judgment of the Title Suit No.68 of 1984. From this it appears that the suit was for-

“ইহা আরজীর তপশীল বর্ণিত নালিশা ভূমিতে বাদীর স্বত্ব থাকা এবং নালিশা ভূমি সংক্রান্ত ৫৮/১৯৬৬-৬৭ নং ই.পি. কেস বেআইনী, যোগযোগী এবং বাদীর উপর বাধ্যকর নহে মর্মে প্রচারাজ্ঞামূলক ডিক্রীর প্রার্থনায় বাদী অত্র মামলা রুজু করিয়াছেন।”

17. From the reading of the plaint of the present suit and from the reading of the Judgment passed by the trial Court in Title Suit No. 68 of 1984 it appears that the cause of action and the reliefs stated in the earlier suit and the present suit are not same. Moreover, the present suit is based on questioning the genuineness of the deed of Kabalas and the decree obtained upon practicing fraud, it cannot be said that the issue involved in the earlier suit and in the present suit are directly and substantially the same by the same parties. It is clear that the present suit stands on different facts and footing with a totally different prayer and in such situation it cannot be said that the issues involved in the present suit have been directly and substantially in issue in the earlier suit and were adjudicated between the same parties.

18. We, therefore, failed to agree with Mr Tobarak Hossain, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners that the suit is barred by res-judicata and the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

19. In the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman, reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217 it has been held by our Appellate Division that,

"The plea of res-judicata is not available in rejecting a plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure- This matter can only be decided on the trial and it cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint, res-judicata can be made an issue in the suit."

20. In the case of Shahabuddin vs Habibur Rahman cited in 50 DLR (AD) 99, it has been held that:

"The question of limitation in a suit is a mixed question of law and fact which can be decided only at the trial on taking evidence. In view of the reliefs prayed in the suit, the plaint cannot be rejected."

21. So, we are therefore, do not agree with the submission of Mr Tabarak Hussain, the learned Advocate for the petitioners that the plaint of the present suit is liable to be rejected upon an application under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that the suit is barred by limitation and res-judicata. We have carefully perused those decision and find that the facts and circumstances of the cases referred by him reported in 10 MLR (AD) 144,10 MLR 2005, 344 and 61 DLR 503 are distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the present case and the same have no manner of application in the present case.

<u>22. From our above discussion and the finding and the decisions cited in the case of Sreemati Pushpa Rani Das vs AKM Habibur Rahman reported in 13 BLD (AD) 217, we are of view that both the question of limitation and of res-judicata raised under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the plaint of the present suit are mixed question of law and fact, which need through investigation on adequate evidence for arriving at a correct decision on framing specific issues by the trial Court.</u>

23. For the reasons stated above, we are of the opinion that the trial Court has rightly rejected the application filed by the defendant petitioners under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned Additional District Judge after giving proper findings concurred with the decision of the trial Court.

24. We do not find any merit in the Rule and the same is liable to be discharged.

25. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

26. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is vacated.

Send a copy of this Judgment to the trial Court below.

End.

full_judgment:
In an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, Rule was issued calling upon opposite parties to show cause as to why the judgment an decree dated 2-6-1998 passed by the Additional District Judge, Rangpur in other Appeal No. 18 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-1996 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Mithapukur, Rangpur in Other Suit No. 48 of 1993 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The opposite party as plaintiffs instituted Miscellaneous Case being No. 48 of 1993 in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Mithapukur for specific performance of contract as well as for a declaration that the registered sale deed executed in favour of the petitioner by the defendant No. 1 is not binding upon opposite party.

3. The case of the plaintiffs stated in the plaint inter-alia is that the land described in the Schedule of the plaint originally belonged to the plaintiff's and proforma-defendant (defendant No. 1) and the plaintiffs-defendant No. 1 were brothers that defendant No. 1 who used to reside in Dhaka decided to transfer his share of the land for a consideration of Taka 85,000 to his brothers; that on 12-1-1990 defendant No. 1 received Taka 55,000 and delivered possession of his share to his brothers in presence of some respected village people on the same date and promised that he would register sale deed as soon as the balance sum would be paid and from that period plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land by cultivating the suit land; that the plaintiffs paid Taka 10,000 on 26-6-1990 and the rest 20,000 on 1-2-1992 and defendant No. 1 agreed to execute register deed in favour of them; that the plaintiffs requested defendant No. 1 time and again to execute a registered sale deed by in vain subsequently defendant No. 1 informed the plaintiffs that he would not execute sale deed if another Taka 20,000 were not paid to defendant No. I; that the plaintiff sent a legal notice to defendant No. 1 through their lawyer on 16-3-1993 but no response was made; that finding no other alternative the plaintiffs filed criminal case No. 68 of 1993 under section 406 and 420 of Penal Code before the Magistrate Court, Mithapukur; that by the enquiry made by the learned Magistrate of the Magistrate Court the Union Parishad Chairman submitted a report regarding their possession in the suit land; that in the meantime the plaintiffs came to know that defendant No.1 executed 2 register sale deeds in favour of defendant No. 2 and 3 (petitioners) on 16-3-1993 of the disputed 1.17-1/2 satak land; that the alleged transfer was collusive, fraudulent and illegal as defendant No.1 has already delivered possession of the suit land to the plaintiffs.

4. The present petitioners contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending inter alia that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, the same is barred by the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence, the suit is barred by limitation and the defendants are bonafide purchasers for value without notice.

5. The case of the defendants in short is that defendant No.1 intended to sale 1.15-1/2 satak of kha schedule and 0.02 satak of Ga schedule land to the petitioners at a consideration of Taka 1,00,100 and executed two separate register sale deeds being 4960 and 4961 dated 16-3-1993 and the petitioner are possessing the suit land by cultivating them; that the plaintiffs being owners of the adjacent land did not institute suit for pre-emption and filed the instant suit for specific performance of contract in order to deprive the petitioners their right; that the petitioner planted some trees and constructed some Kutcha huts over the suit land; that the petitioner filed additional written statement dated 17-10-1993 which was recorded in the file.

6. Both the parties adduced evidence both oral and documentary. The trial Court after hearing the parties and considering the facts and circumstances decreed the suit. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court the present petitioner as appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 1996 before the District Judge, Rangpur and the same was heard and disposed of by the Additional District Judge, Rangpur who vide impugned judgment and decree dismissed the appeal and thereby affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court the petitioner moved before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

8. Ms Nahid Mahatab, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that both the Courts below without applying their judicial mind and without considering the facts and circumstances and provision of law most illegally and in an arbitrary manner decreed the suit and thereby the Courts below committed an error occasioning failure of justice. She submits that both the Courts below misread the evidence as well as misinterpreted the law and thereby caused substantial injustice to the petitioners who are bonafide purchasers and protected by section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act and as such both the Courts below without considering the case of the petitioners decreed the suit causing substantial injustice. The learned Advocate by referring the plaint as well as the impugned judgment submits that this case specific performance of contract is solely based on oral contract and whenever a suit is being pressed on the basis of oral contract heavy duty cast upon the plaintiff to prove the same in accordance with law which is very much absence in the case in hand. She submits that all the PWs are interested witnesses as well as the evidence namely documentary evidence upon which the Courts below relied relates to a criminal case which is not admissible in a civil proceeding. Apart from that she submits that the present petitioners are bonafide purchasers established their case that they had no knowledge about the earlier oral agreement and as such they have protected as per the provision of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. She also submits that the alleged oral agreement was entered in the year 1990 but the plaintiff kept silent till 1993 which clearly shows that just to frustrated the registered deed of the petitioners the plaintiff instituted the present suit in hand. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred the decisions reported in 40 DLR 271, 3 BLD 258, 17 BLD (AD) 328 = 50 DLR (AD) 13 , 36 DLR (AD) 248 and 5 MLR (AD) 171 = 5 BLC (AD) 97,

9. At the instant of the petitioner the matter has been fixed on 23-2-2010 and heard in part on 25-2-2010 and also same was heard on 2-3-2010 and today is fixed for judgment but despite that no one appears on behalf of the opposite party to oppose the Rule.

10. I have perused the impugned judgment and decree, revisional application, grounds taken there- on, decisions as referred to and heard the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

11. On perusal of the same, it appears that the opposite party as plaintiffs instituted the suit in hand for specific performance of contract on the ground that on 19-1-1990 they have entered an oral agreement with defendant No. 1 and they have paid the consideration in different occasions as well as praying for a decree that the sale deed executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of the present petitioner defendants are not binding upon them. During trial the plaintiffs adduced 4 witnesses including the plaintiffs and mother. The plaintiffs also adduced some proceeding of criminal cases as well as 2 hand written letters. On perusal of the same it appears that the main contention of the plaintiffs are that the defendant No.1 used to reside in Dhaka who offered to sale the property in question and accordingly they paid the entire amount to the defendant No. 1 and his son but the defendant No. 1 failed to executed the sale deed and in the meantime the defendant No. 1 sold the same to the petitioner. On perusal of the same it appears that the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court considered the evidence and decreed the suit.

12. It is now a well settled provision of law is that exercising the, power conferred under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court can- not go in to the factual aspect even in a case of reversal of judgment and decree otherwise the petitioner can show any misreading or misinterpretation of law and fact which effecting the ultimate result of the Courts below. In the present case in hand the petitioner raised the question of misreading of evidence as well as misinterpretation of law.

13. On perusal of the impugned judgment and decree it appears that the Courts below mostly relied upon the documents of a criminal proceeding, In the case Mamud Raja Bhuiyan vs Md Lal Miah reported in 40 DLR 271 the High Court Division held as follows;

"Thirdly, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contended that the judgment of the appellate Court is based on judgments of Criminal cases Exhibits 3 and 4. It is true that the appellate Court has considered the judgments of the criminal Courts Exhibits 3 and 4 and has held that the present defendant No. I could not prove his possession in the suit land. The appellate Court further observed that in the judgment of the criminal motion (Exhibit 4) it has been observed that the present defendants failed to prove their possession of the land. So, on the basis of the above inadmissible evidence, the appellate Court has decided the question of possession against the defendants. It must be remembered that the criminal Courts finding of possession is not admissible in evidence in a civil suit. So the appellate Court erred in law in taking into account the findings of the possession of the suit land given by the criminal Courts in Exhibits 3 and 4 and as such the judgment is bad in law and liable to be aside. This view finds support from the case of SN Gupta & Co vs Sadananda Ghosh reported in 11 DLR 470. wherein it has been held by the Division Bench of the then Dhaka High Court as follows;

"The findings of criminal Courts are not admissible in evidence in civil suits".

So it appears that use of papers and documents adduced in a criminal proceeding is discouraged in a civil proceeding specially when the same is relates to declaration of title or relates dispute in respect of any property.

14. In the present case in hand the plaintiffs raised their claim on the strength of an oral agreement. In support of the agreement the plaintiffs adduced oral evidence but on scrutiny of the same it appears that all are admittedly interested witnesses. Apart from that they have adduced 2 letters but in support of that letters no material evidence has been adduced by the plaintiffs as because the same was not posted or delivered or by any admitted procedure. Regarding specific performance of oral contract, the Appellate Division in a case of Md Moslemuddin vs Md Jonab Ali reported in 17 BLD (AD) 328 = 50 DLR (AD) 13 held as follows:

"We should observe here that so far as the oral agreement is concerned it should always be closely scrutinized and taken with a grain of suit. Although oral agreement is not barred by any law it has to be looked at with some suspicion unless proved by very reliable evidence and circumstances. In Ouseph Varghese vs Joseph Aley. (1969) 2 SCWR 347 Supreme Court of India discouraged a decree for specific performance of a contract on the basis of an agreement supported solely by oral evidence".

15. In the case of Santosh Kumar Chakrabarty vs MA Motaleb Hossain reported in 36 DLR (AD) 248 their Lordships held as follows:

"Mr Rafique-ul-Huq contends that whether the summons was duly served or not is a question of fact and the finding arrived at by, the trial Court on this question cannot be interfered with in revision. But this finding is found to have resulted from glaring misconception of law as well as non-consideration of material evidence and as such is not immune from interference in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court Division in the circumstance rightly interfered therewith. The appeal from this judgment must fail. In the  result, the appeal is dismissed without however any cost".

16. So it appears that where there is serious misinterpretation or glaring illegally apparent on the basis of the record the High Court Division has ample jurisdiction to interfere, even both the Courts below passed judgment of affirmance. In the case reported in 5 MLR (AD) 171 = 5 BLC (AD) 97, also the Appellate Division came to a conclusion that in exceptional circumstances such as consideration or misreading of material evidence on record or of on evidence resulting in an error occasioning failure of justice, the High Court Division can exercise its revisional jurisdiction. So, it appears that while deciding a suit for specific performance of contract based on oral agreement a heavy duty cast upon the plaintiff to prove the same beyond all reasonable doubt. In the case in hand it appears that the Courts below relied upon basically the proceeding of a criminal case and oral evidence as well as 2 letters. But it appears that there is no scope to adduced papers relates to any criminal proceeding in a civil dispute. Apart from that it appears from the plaint reading of the evidence namely the oral evidence it appears that all the PW are closely related and highly interested witnesses. Apart from that it appears that the letters as annexed by the plaintiffs as evidence are hand written and not delivered in due process. None was examine to prove the said letter's genuineness strictly in accordance with law. Admitted the defendant No. 1 the vendor of the present petitioner did not contested of the suit but at the same time it is duty of the plaintiff to prove his case beyond all reasonable doubt. Any weakness of the defendant cannot be act as aid in favour of the plaintiff to prove his case. It further appears that the agreement as alleged was entered in the year 1990 and on several days payments were made but till 1993 the plaintiffs kept silent which also creates serious doubt in the plaintiffs' case.

17. Section 27 of the Specific Relief Act deals with the provision regarding relief against parties and persons claiming under them by subsequent title. Section 27(b) of the said Act runs as follows:

"Relief against parties and persons claiming under them by subsequent title-Except as otherwise provided by this Chapter, specific performance of a contract may be enforced against-

(a) Either party thereto;

(b) Any other person claiming under him by a title arising subsequently to the contract, except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract".

<u>18. So it appears that a Specific Performance of contract can be enforced against any person claiming under him by a title arising subsequent to the contract except transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. In the case in hand the defendant petitioners by sufficient evidence proved that they were not aware of any such contract in any manner and after filing of the suit they came to know about the said oral transaction. Apart from that the plaintiffs who are acting as bargadar under defendant No. 1 and subsequently the defendant No.2 and 3 took advantage of the same and instituted the suit. It has been mentioned earlier that ordinary this Court exercising the power conferred under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot interference in a concurrent finding of fact. But in the case in hand it appears that the Courts below not only misread the evidence but also misinterpreted the provision of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. Obviously the onus is upon the defendant purchasers who claimed the protection of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act and in the case in hand by adducing 4 witnesses the defendants proved that they are transferee for value who paid the money in good faith and without notice of the original contract. Apart from the doubt regarding the oral contract the provision of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act is also applicable in the case in hand.</u>

19. While adjudicating the appeal as well as the suit the Courts below also came to a conclusion about the deed executed in favour of the petitioners as they failed to produce the original one. Though the petitioners categorically stated that soon after the registration the plaintiffs institute the suit and as per normal practice it took some time to get the original deed and apart from that in the absence of any allegation of fraud, collusiveness the certified copy is always admissible as secondary evidence. In the present case in hand the plaintiffs though prayed for a declaration that the deeds executed in favour of the petitioners defendant are not binding but there is no evidence to show that the said deeds are being obtained by the petitioners defendant from the defendant No. 1 in collusion or by practicing fraud or to frustrated the oral agreement. In the case in hand the plaintiffs also failed to show by any credible evidence that the subsequent deed which are registered in accordance with law are obtained in collusion which is a mandatory provision of law to succeeds in a suit where in a decree as prayed against such instruments.

20. Considering the facts and circumstances. provision of law and the decisions as referred to, it appears that both Courts below while deciding the suit misread the evidence as there is doubt regarding the genuineness of the oral agreement as because in numerous decisions this Court as well as of our Apex Court came to a conclusion that the Court should apply its judicial mind very cautiously while dealing with an oral agreement. Apart from that it appears that the petitioners successfully the proved their case under section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act. In such circumstances, I am of the view that both the Courts below without applying their judicial mind and by misinterpreting the law and misreading the evidence decreed the suit which is not tenable in the eye of law.

Accordingly, I find substance in this Rule. The Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree passed by the Additional District Judge, Rangpur in other Appeal No. 18 of 1996 dated 2-6-1998 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31-1-1996 passed by Senior Assistant Judge, in Other Suit No. 48 of 1993 is hereby set aside. The suit is stand dismissed.

Send down the LC record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Abul Kalam Maijuddin, Advocate------ For the Petitioners.
Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, Advocate------ For the Opposite Parties,
parties:
Abani Kumar Mistry and others ------ Petitioners
vs
Government of the Peoples and Republic of Bangladesh and others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued on an application for revision made by the plaintiff-petitioner under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code) against the judgment and decree dated 29-2-2000 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No. 3, Khulna in Title Appeal No. 318 of 1994 reversing the judgment and decree dated 12-5-1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in Title Suit No, 105 of 1978.

2. The plaintiffs (petitioners herein) filed Title Suit No, 105 of 1978 against the defendants for declaration of title in the suit land,

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit land originally belonged to Priya Mondal. During his possession, he died leaving 2 minor sons namely, Pagla Mondal and Lalit Mondal. One Haribala Mondal, uncle of Pagla Mondal and Lalit Mondal, settled 22 areas of land with Sreemanta Mistry by registered patta dated 12-4-1928, Haribala Mondal again settled 1.75 acres of land by registered patta dated 5-4-1928 in favour of Sreemanta Mondal. One Krishna Mondal also settled 2.50 acres of land in favour of Sreemanta Mistry and In this way Sreemanta Mistry acquired total 5.37 acres of land, During his possession, he died leaving three sons, namely, Saradakanta Mistry, Barada Kanta Mistry and Aswani Mistry. There was dispute among the co-sharers and plaintiff No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 for partition and declaration of title and the suit was decreed on compromise on 7-9-1958. Through Advocate Commissioner, the plaintiffs of that suit got possession of5.36 acres instead of 5.37 acres of land. Barada Kanta Mistry died leaving two sons, plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 and Aswani Mistry died leaving 3 sons, plaintiff Nos. 4-6. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land but the SA Khatian was wrongly prepared in' the name of defendant Nos. 3, 5, 6 and father of defendant No. 4, namely, Kritiram Mandai, The defendants have no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. Defendant Nos. 1-3 most illegally included the suit land in the list of vested and non-resident property and the same was illegally leased out to defendant Nos. 7-10. The cause of action arose on 15th of Magh, 1384 BS. When defendant Nos. 1-3 and 7-10 threatened the plaintiffs to dispossess them from the suit land. For the reasons stated, the plaintiffs filed the suit.

4. Defendant Nos. 1-2 and 11 contested the suit by filing separate written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint. The case of the contesting defendants, in short, is that defendant Nos. 3-6 left this country for India and that they started living in India and that, as such, the suit land was correctly enlisted in the list of vested and non-resident property. Thereafter, the suit land was leased out to defendant Nos. 3-10 and that the lessees were in possession of the suit land. The plaintiffs obtained compromise decree in Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 by practicing fraud upon the Court. The Government was not made party to that suit. The present plaintiffs filed the suit with a malafide intention to grab the suit land. For the reasons stated the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. Defendant Nos. 14 and 15, 16, and 7, 12, and 13, 18 and 20 also filed written statements but ultimately, they did not contest the suit and the appeal. They however, supported the case of the plaintiffs.

6. On the pleadings various issues were framed including maintainability of the suit, limitation, whether or not the suit was barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and whether or not the suit was barred under the principle of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence and whether or not the plaintiffs were entitled to get any relief as prayed for.

7. The plaintiffs examined 3 PWs and the defendant examined 6 DWs. The plaintiffs adduced documents which were marked as Exhibit Nos. 1-3(a) and the documents adduced by the defendant Nos. 1-3 were marked as Exhibit Nos. Ka and Kha series. The documents adduced by defendant No.4 were marked as Exhibit Nos. A-B(1).

8. The trial Court decreed the suit. On an appeal therefrom at the instance of the contesting defendants the, Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit reversing the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge.

9. Being aggrieved by, and dissatisfied with, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, the plaintiff-petitioners obtained the instant Rule from this Court

10. Mr Abul Kalam Mainuddin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners, submits that the Court of appeal below failed to properly assess the evidence on record and that came to an erroneous finding that the plaintiffs had no right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. He further submits that the Court of appeal below failed to discuss the evidence led by the parties and that the Court of appeal below also utterly failed to give its finding about the possession of the suit land. He lastly, submits that the Court of appeal below reversed the judgment of the trial Court without adverting to the findings of the trial Court with proper reasonings.

11. Mr Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite parties, submits that the Court of appeal below considering the evidence on record correctly held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. He further submits that in Title Suit No. 218 of 1951, the plaintiffs did not implead the Government as party to the suit and that the plaintiffs obtained a compromise decree by practicing fraud upon the Court. He also submits that the parties of Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 and that of the parties of the present suit are the same and that, as such, the present suit is barred under section 11 of the Code. He lastly submits that the plaintiffs filed the instant suit with ulterior motive to grab the suit land.

12. Perused the judgments of both the Courts below and the record.

13. It appears that the trial Court discussed the evidence on record and held that the plaintiffs got possession of 5.36 acres of land on the basis of the compromise decree obtained in Title Suit No. 218 of  1951. The trial Court further held that as the suit was decreed on compromise, there was no necessity for giving delivery of possession by the Advocate Commissioner through Courts. The trial Court also held that the plaintiffs filed the pattra dated 11-4-25 and 12-4-25 executed by Krishna Mondal and Haribala Mondal respectively in favour of Sreemanta Mistry (Exhibit 2 series.) and that came to a definite finding that the land was. settled with Sreemanta Mistry by Haribala, Mondal and Lalit Mondal The trial Court disbelieved the possession of the lessees and held that since the plaintiffs were living in the country, their property could not be legally enlisted as vested and non resident property, The trial Court held that the plaintiffs had cause of action and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The trial Court, therefore, held that there was no difficulty to declare that the plaintiffs had title in the suit land.

14. The Court of appeal below, on the other hand, discussed the evidence on record and held that PW 1 admitted in his cross-examination that he had no knowledge about the pattra of Sreemanta Mistry, PW 1 also stated that he had no knowledge about the suit land. The Court of appeal below also held that 'the plaintiffs filed the suit for 5.37 acres of land, but in Title Suit No. 218 of 1951, the plaintiffs were allotted saham to the extent of 5.36 acres of Iand. The Court of appeal below held that in Title Suit No. 218 of 1951, the plaintiffs did not implead the Government as party to the suit and that, as such, the decree of that suit was not binding upon the Government. The Court of appeal below also held that the parties in Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 and that the parties in the present Title Suit were the same. Therefore, the Court of appeal below held that the plaintiffs could not file the suit twice against the same persons for the self-same relief. The Court of appeal below also held that Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 was decreed in preliminary form on 23-9-1958 and that there was no reason that the names of the plaintiffs should not be recorded in the SA khatian as the SA record was prepared in 1960 in the locality. The Court of appeal below also held that PW 1 stated that he used to possess 5,37 acrees of land which land he got by way of pattra from Sreemanta, but the plaintiffs failed to produce any dakhila in support of their claim. So, the Court of appeal below held that the pattra, Exhibit 2, series were not acted upon. The Court of appeal below discussed the evidence in detail and held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land. The Court of appeal below considering the evidence on record held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their right, title interest and possession in the suit land.

<u>15. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that the trial Court did not give any finding that the plaintiffs were in possession of the suit land. The trial Court without discussing the evidence on record, abruptly held that as the plaintiffs had cause of action and that as the suit was not barred by limitation, the plaintiffs were entitled to get a decree as prayed for. But the trial Court came to the above finding without discussing the evidence at all. The Court of appeal below, on the other hand, discussed the evidence on record elaborately and held that since the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 and since the parties of that suit and the parties of the present suit are common the plaintiffs could not file subsequent suit for the self-same relief against the self-same persons. The Court of appeal below came to a definite finding that the predecessor of the plaintiffs did not acquire any title on the basis of the pattra. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referred the case of Laxmi Kama Roy vs Upazila Nirbahi Officer and others 46 DLR 136 and submitted that since the law on enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance 1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974, no further vested property case could be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead. In reply, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties referred the case of Ms Dulichand Omraolal vs Bangladesh, through the Secretary, Ministry of Industries and others, 33 DLR (AD) 30 and submitted that once a property assumed the character of 'enemy property' during the period from 6-9-1965 to 16-2-1969, the subsequent taking over of the property as 'enemy property', was permissible in law.</u>

16. In the case referred to above, the Appellate Division has held as follows:

"If any action is sought to be taken with regard to any property after 16-2-1969 as enemy property, it is to be seen whether the property sought to be taken over as enemy property was so between 6-9-1965 and 16-2-1969, the promulgation and revocation of Proclamation of Emergency. If at any time during the currency of the Emergency with the Defence of Pakistan Ordinance and the Rules remaining in full force, the property comes within the definition of 'enemy property' it continues to remain so, even though actual steps might not have been taken by the appropriate authority to take it over and so, the authority, whether the Custodian or Additional. Custodian or Assistant Custodian or Board, may, for the management and control and vesting or transfer, either under Rule 181 or 182 of the Defence of Pakistan Rules take action. It is to be observed that an individual or a property becomes an 'enemy' or 'enemy property' by operation of law on the fulfilment of the conditions laid down by the relevant Defence of Pakistan Rules and no further formal declaration by an officer or authority is needed and once a property comes within the definition of 'enemy property' within the period of 6-9-65 to 16-2-69 subsequent taking over of such property is permissible, but not otherwise."

17. From the above decision of Ute Appellate Division, it is clear that if a property assumed the character of 'enemy property' during the period from 6-9-1965 to 16-2-1969 the subsequent taking over of the property as 'enemy property' is permissible in law.

18. It also appears that the plaintiffs filed Title Suit No. 218 of 1951 for declaration of title and for partition. In that Title Suit No. 218 of 1951, Sarada Kanta, Barada Kanta, Aswini, all sons of Sreemanta Mistry, were the plaintiffs. In the said suit, Monoranjan Mondal was a defendant and in the instant suit his son Satish is defendant No.3. In the said suit Kalipada Mondal was defendant No. 5(ka) and in the instant suit he is defendant No. 14 in the said suit Gurupada Mondal, son of Pagal. Mondal was defendant No. 7(ka) and in the instant suit he is defendant No. 15. In the said suit Ruplal Mondal was defendant No. 13 and in the, instant suit his son Matlal Mondal is defendant No 12. Therefore, the plaintiffs cannot pray for declaration of title in the suit property against the self-same defendant in the present Title Suit No. 105 of 1978.

19. It appears from the record that plaintiff No.1 Sarada Kanta Mistry filed an application on 6- 7-1978 before the then Sub-Divisional. Officer, Khulna, praying for lease of suit property admitting the suit land as 'vested property'. His prayer for taking lease of the property was rejected on 15-8-1978. Therefore he cannot claim that the suit property is not vested property and that his claim is barred under section 115 of the Evidence Act.

20. Considering the evidence on record the Court of appeal below as the final Court of facts held that the plaintiffs failed to prove their right, title, interest and possession in the suit land. This finding of the Court of appeal below cannot be interfered with by this Court unless it is found that the finding of the Court of appeal below is perverse for non-consideration and misreading of evidence by the Court of appeal below. In support of this contention, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties referred the case of Kochi Mia alias Khocha Mia vs Suruj Mia being dead his heirs Md Fazlur Rahman and others 51 DLR (AD) 57. In the case referred to above, the Appellate Division has held that the High Court Division as a revisional Court had hardly any jurisdiction to set aside 'the finding of facts arrived at by the appellate Court and that also without discussing any fault in the factual finding by the said Court. Similar view has also been expressed in the case of Shamser Ali (Md) and others Vs Mosammat Katizad Bibi 44 DLR (AD) 231 In the case referred to above the Appellate Division has held that the High Court Division set aside the finding, of the appellate Court on a review of the evidence and thereby committed an error in law when there was no consideration of evidence and misconstruction of the document. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners however failed to show that there was any misreading or non-consideration of evidence or misconstruction of the documents by the Court of appeal below:

21. Under the circumstances, I find that the reasoning arrived at and the decision made by the Court of appeal below do not suffer from any illegality or error of law warranting interference by this Court exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code.

22. For the reasons stated, I do not find any substance in this Rule.

23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The order of status quo passed at the time of issuance of the Rule is hereby recalled and vacated.

24. There is no order as to costs.

Send down the lower Court record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mainur Reza Chowdhury J: This leave petition arises out of judgment and order of the High Court Division in Civil Revision 3617 of 1995 discharging the Rule.

2. The petitioners as the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 33 of 1984 in the First Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Sadar, Chittagong which was renumbered as Title Suit No. 72 of 1985 after being transferred to . the second Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Chittagong. The petitioners filed the above suit against the respondent for declaration of title, confirmation of possession and for permanent injunction. The case of the petitioners was that the names of their predecessors were recorded in CS and RS Khatian but in the PS and BS Khatian the names of the respondents was recorded and the Government claimed the said property.

3. The aforesaid suit was decreed ex parte on 20-2-1986 and respondent filed Miscellaneous Case No. 28 of 1986 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was dismissed on contest on 19-6-1986 and against the aforesaid order dated 19-6-1986 the respondent filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1987. The said appeal was also dismissed for default on 30-7-1992. On 16-4-1984 Government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1994 under Order XLI rule 19 CPC along with an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act praying for condoning the delay. The petitioners resisted the same by filing written objection. The learned Additional District Judge by judgment and order dated 27-7-1995 allowed the Miscellaneous Case by setting aside the order of the dismissal and restored the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 107 of 1987 to its file and number. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order dated 27-7-1995 the respondent as petitioner moved the High Court Division. The point for consideration in the Rule by the High Court Division was whether there was any error in the impugned judgment in allowing' the Miscellaneous Case or restoring the appeal. it appears that there was delay of 574 days in filing Miscellaneous Case No. 2 of 1994 before the learned Additional District Judge and the respondent filed an application under section. 5 of the Limitation Act praying for condonation of delay explaining the reason for the delay. The High Court Division after detailed discussion of the reason for the filing the Miscellaneous Case and the oral evidence was satisfied with the explanation.

<u>4. The High Court Division observed that there was normally no difference between the Government as the litigant and a public litigant in case of considering an application under section 5 of the Limitation Act. However, following the principles laid down in several decisions referred to in the judgment the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division was of the opinion that some consideration in appropriate circumstances may be extended to Government appearing as a litigant. In the instant case it was found that the Government had given satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the Miscellaneous Case and that there was substantial Government interest i.e. public interest, involved in the case and, as such, the learned Additional District Judge considering the facts and circumstances passed the impugned judgment and order condoning the delay thereby allowed the application filed under Order XLI rule 19 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court Division on perusal of the impugned judgment and in view of the reasons. stated in the judgment which is essentially a decision on facts, did not think that the impugned order calls for interference and therefore discharged the Rule.</u>

5. We do not find any illegality or infirmity in the judgment of the High Court Division.

The petition is therefore, dismissed.

End.
