full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: In these Rules common questions of law of public importance are involved. The points are, whether (1) the Artha Rin Adalats (the Adalat) while executing decree(s) can issue warrant of arrest or order for detention in civil imprisonment of judgment debtons if they fail to pay the decretal amount without exhausting the provisions in section 33 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 (the Ain of 2003), and section 51 and Order XXI, rule 37, Civil Procedure Code (the Code), (2) the executing Adalat(s) can issue such process or order of detention in civil imprisonment against women judgment debtor(s), and (3) the Adalat(s) can issue such process or order for civil imprisonment directly under sub-section (10) without exhausting sub-section (9) of section 34 of the Ain of 2003.

2. We have been noticing inconsistent orders are being made by the Adalat(s) in this regard. In some cases the Adalats have been making orders for civil prison of judgment debtor(s) for a period of six months without assigning any reasons whatsoever on the asking of the decree holder(s) as if they were doing routine works. In some cases the Adalat(s) have been issuing such orders directly without taking steps for recovery of the decreed money by selling the mortgaged property and, in some cases, the orders have been made against all the members of a family including women and children. In some cases attempts were made to sell the property in auction but as none participated in the auction, the Adalat(s) issued orders on the prayer of the decree holder(s).

3. The first statute on the same subject was the Artha Rin Ordinance, 1989 (Ordinance No. XVI of 1989) promulgated on 13th November 1989 with the object for realisation of loan by the financial organisations from the defaulter debtor(s). The said Ordinance became an Act of Parliament on l 0th January 1990 under the name the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 (the Ain of 1990). This Ain of 1990 was repealed on 10th March 2003 and in its place the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, (the Ain of 2003) came into force on 1st May 2003. This being a special law and it was promulgated in suppression of all preexisting laws for the recovery of money by the financial organisations from the defaulters of loans, it should have been spoken of as a model piece of legislation as the premier law on the subject. The realisation of outstanding debts from the debtor(s) by financial organisations being a complex sociological problem, the legislature should not have taken hasty steps in promulgating them in the manner It had taken on the subject.

4. It is worth to mention that there was no proper groundwork of the law at the time of its promulgation by circulating to the judges, lawyers, and academicians for opinion with a view to detect errors, omissions and imperfections that might exist in the draft law before it was passed into law. Two enactments have been promulgated within a space of fourteen years on the same subject, and the present law has been amended within one year of its implementation. The Adalat(s) are therefore, confused and making conflicting orders. Since we find no uniformity in the orders and huge number of revision petitions and writ petitions are being filed by the litigants taking advantage of the ambiguity of the orders, we feel it proper to decide the points on a thorough examination of the relevant laws so that the Adalat(s) would be able to get a guideline while dealing with the similar matter. As there is public importance on the subject, we requested Mr Mahmudul Islam and Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocates to assist this Court for resolving the said points as amicus curiae. Mr Mahmudul Islam has made well-thought comprehensive arguments covering the relevant laws. We have also heard Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Janata Bank, Mr Shahid Alam learned Advocate on behalf of the Pubali Bank Ltd and the learned Advocates for the petitioners.

5. In this statute there are 8 chapters. Chapter 1 contains 3 sections, the name, the definition and the supremacy of the Ain of 2003 over other laws. Chapter II contains the establishment of the Artha Rin Adalat is Chapter III contains the powers and jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalats, Chapter IV contains the institution of the suit(s) and the procedure of the Adalat(s) in holding trial of suits, Chapter V contains the settlement conference which is almost similar to Alternative Dispute Resolution, Chapter VI contains the procedure for execution of the decree(s), Chapter VII contains the provision for appeal and revision and Chapter VIII contains miscellaneous matters about the settlement of disputes besides those contained in Chapter V even after disposal of the suite(s). We are concerned about Chapters VI and VII for arriving at a decision on the points.

8. Sub-section (1) of section 34 authorises the Adalat(s) to detain the judgment debtor(s) in civil prison upto six months on the application of the decree holder(s) for compelling him to pay the decretal money. In sub-section (2) there is prohibition for making such order of detention in civil prison against the heirs of the judgment debtor if the judgment debtor dies and his heirs are substituted. This power can also be exercised against the share holders of companies and partnership firms if any execution case is filed against a company, partnership firm or corporate body, treating them as natural person. Sub-section (5) states that the detained person shall not be released from the prison unless he pays the entire decretal money or undergoes the entire period of six months and that as soon as he pays the decretal money he will be released forthwith. There is provision for interim release from detention in sub-section (6), which provides that notwithstanding anything provided in sub-section (5), if the judgment debtor pays 25% of the decretal money and executes a bond promising to pay the balance amount within ninety days, he will be released from civil prison. There is further prohibition for detention of judgment debtor(s) in sub-section (9) which provides that such order cannot be made unless at least one auction sale of the property is held and that by reason of such sale the decree holder's(s) dues are fully recovered. There is further restriction to detain judgment-debtor(s) under the age of 18 (eighteen) years. There is another provision that a judgment-debtor cannot be detained in prison again if he undergoes civil prison for six months even if there are more than one execution proceedings for recovery of the decretal money under the Ain.

9. Sub-section (10), however states that if for any reason there is no possibility of holding one auction sale in accordance with sub-section (9), the judgment debtor can be arrested directly and detained in prison. Mr Mahmudul Islam submits that this provision is equivalent to the proviso to clauses (a) and (b) of section 51 and the proviso to sub-rule (1) of rule 37 of order XXI. Under the aforesaid provisions, in execution of a money decree, if the Court is satisfied that the judgment debtor is obstructing the execution or delaying the execution by any means or is trying to leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, it shall record the reasons and order for detention of the judgment debtor. We find substance in the contention of the learned Advocate.

10. On a reading of the Ain of 2003 no inference may be drawn other than that the legislature while promulgating this Ain kept in view the following basic considerations:

(a) speedy recovery of loan from indigent but dishonest debtor(s) of loan through special Courts of civil nature, namely the Artha Rin Adalats :

(b) a defaulter and guarantor of loan should get a fair trial and the execution proceeding(s) to be disposed of in accordance with the accepted principles of natural justice;

(c) every effort should be made to avoid delay in the trial and execution proceedings;

(d) the procedure should not be complicated and should, to the utmost extent possible, ensure fair deal to the poorer debtor(s).

11. In the preamble the object for promulgating the Ain has been spelt out "আর্থিক প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক ঋণ আদায়ের জন্য প্রচলিত আইনের অধিকতর সংশোধন ও সংহতকরন কল্পে প্রণীত আইন।”  The purpose and object of this piece of legislation is discernible from the preamble. When the object of an Act as given in the preamble is "to consolidate and amend the law", such Act consolidates not only the pre-existing enactment, but also amends the law on the subject and this means both addition to and derogation from the pre-existing law. It follows that such an Act is a complete Code in itself as regards the subject it deals with. In other words, where an amending and codifying law deals with a certain subject, it must be generally taken that the law is exhaustive on the subject to the extent to which it has dealt with. But, in this particular legislation, it is seen, the legislature was unmindful in promulgating an exhaustive law, for reasons best known to them, and failed to codify a complete code which is evident from sections 5(2), 6(1), 21(4), 22(7), 26, 32(1),40 of the Ain. A complete Code has three characteristics that distinguish it from ordinary legislation, such as (a)completeness in containing all the laws in force governing the subject of which it treats; (b) logical, scientific and, at the same time, convenient arrangement; and (c) clear and concise phraseology, which avoids prolixity on the one hand and ambiguity on the other. (2 Encyclopaedia: social sciences, 606).

12. Where a complete procedure is provided in any enactment for the disposal of disputes it is that procedure that must be followed and not the one prescribed by the Code. Where an enactment provides a special procedure only for some matters, its provisions must apply in regard to those matters and the provisions of the Code will apply for matters on which the enactment is silent. The Code of Civil Procedure consists of (a) statutes, (b) adjudications, and (c) customs, as supplemented by necessary amendments to give it completeness, Thus, the Code is exhaustive of the subject it treats of; but an Act is not so. An Act is derived from a statute. Therefore, it is this mixed character of the Code that distinguishes it from an Act. It is, therefore, not for a judge to disregard or go outside the enactment according to its true construction. Lord Halsbury observed:

"where a statute is expressly said to codify the law, you are not at liberty to go outside the Code so created because before the existence of that Code another law prevailed."

13. Jurists are of the view that in the absence of any provision on any particular matter, the Court may act on the principle that every procedure is perm is sible till law prohibits it. In Wilhe, (1955)2 SCR 1140 it has been observed that in a case for which there is no express provision in the Code or where there is ambiguity, the Court is to see whether there has been substantial compliance with the Code and the bounds of extension are an express prohibition and prejudice beyond which it cannot go.

14. In the Code we notice the procedure for detaining a judgment debtor in execution of the money decree in section 51 and Order XXI, rule 37. Section 55 relates to the manner of arrest and detention of a judgment debtor and section 56 prohibits arrest or detention of a woman in execution of a decree for money. Section 51 reads as follows:

"51. Subject to such conditions and limitations as may be prescribed, the Court may, on the application of the decree holder, order execution of the decree-

(a) by delivery of any property specifically decreed;

(b) by attachment and sale or by sale without attachment of any property;

(c) by arrest and detention in prison;

(d) by appointing a receiver; or

(e) in such other manner as the nature of the relief granted may require;

Provided that, where the decree is for the payment of money, execution by detention in prison shall not be ordered unless, after giving the judgment debtor an opportunity of showing cause why he should not be committed to prison,  the Court, for reasons recorded in writing, is satisfied-

(a) That the judgment-debtor, with the object or effect of obstructing or delaying the execution of the decree,

(i) is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court, or

(ii) has, after the institution of the suit in which the decree was passed, dishonestly transferred, concealed or removed any part of his property, or committed any other act of bad faith in relation to his property; or

(b) That the judgment debtor has, or has had since the date of the decree, the means to pay the amount of the decree or some substantial part thereof and refuses or neglects or has refused or neglected to pay the same, or

(c) That the decree is for a sum for which the judgment debtor was bound in a fiduciary capacity to account.

Section 56 reads:

"56. Notwithstanding anything in this part, the Court shall not order the arrest or detention in the civil prison of a woman in execution of a decree for the payment of money".

Order XXI, rule 37 reads as follows:

"(1) Notwithstanding anything in these rules, where an application is for the execution of a decree for the payment of money by the arrest and detention in the civil prison of a judgment debtor who is liable to be arrested in pursuance of the application, the Court shall instead of issuing a warrant for his arrest, issue a notice calling upon him to appear before the Court on a day to be specified in the notice and show cause why he should not be committed to the civil prison.

Provided that such notice shall not be necessary if the Court is satisfied by affidavit, or otherwise, that, with the object or effect of delaying the execution of the decree, the judgment debtor is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court.

(2) Where appearance is not made in obedience to the notice, the Court shall, if the decree holder so requires, issue a warrant for the arrest of the judgment-debtor."

15. In view of section 4 of the Code, section 51 must be read subject to any conditions and limitations which may be prescribed by the Ain of 2003. Section 51 simply states generally the powers of the Court to enforce execution and the details are relegated to Order XXI. The object of these provisions is to protect indigent but honest debtor(s). These provisions authorise the civil Court to issue warrant of arrest or civil. imprisonment if the judgment debtor fails to pay the decretal money but before issuing warrant of arrest the Court is required to issue a show cause notice calling upon him to explain why he should, not be committed to civil prison. The object of this provision is to afford protection to honest debtor(s) who are incapable of paying their dues for reason beyond their control and who have not committed any act of bad faith. The conditions of rule 37 of Order XXI are conceived in the interest of protection of liberty and freedom of the judgment debtorts which the Code considers to be of paramount importance and are to be construed as mandatory violations of which invariably, results in vitiating the consequential order. If the decree holder(s) seeks for imprisonment of the judgment debtor(s), the Court is bound to issue in the first instance, a notice to the judgment debtor(s) to appear and show cause why they should not be committed to civil prison in execution of the decree unless the Court decides to dispense with the notice under the proviso to sub-rule (1). It is only when no appearance is made in obedience of the notice that the Court can issue a warrant of arrest under sub-rule (2). The proviso empowers the Court to dispense with the notice If the Court is satisfied by affidavit or otherwise that the conditions mentioned therein exist and to record reasons that the judgment debtor is likely to abscond or leave the local limits of the jurisdiction of the Court with the object of delaying the execution of the decree. Where the judgment debtor(s) had the means but was unwilling to repay the debts, the Court can order his arrest in execution of the decree(s).

16. Section 51 declares that if the debtor(s) have no means to pay they cannot be arrested and detained unless they are given an opportunity of Showing cause why they should not be committed to prison. If they still refuse or neglect to honour their obligation or if they commit acts of bad faith, they incur liability of imprisonment. This implies, there must be some element of bad faith beyond mere indifference to pay, some deliberate or recusant disposition in the past or, alternatively, current means to pay the decree. This provision emphasises the need to establish not mere omission to pay but an attitude of refusal on demand verging on dishonest disowning of the obligation under the decree.

17. This provision is practically akin to the principle what is commonly known as audi alteram partem rule. It says that no one should be condemned unheard. Notice is the first limb of this principle. It must be precise and unambiguous. It should apprise the party disclosing only the case he has to meet. There must be an investigation to be made by the executing Court regarding the current ability of the judgment debtors to pay off their outstanding debts or their malafide refusal, if any, to discharge the debts.

18. Though the executing Court has been authorised to issue order of arrest or detention of civil prison subject to fulfillment of certain conditions, such power does not extend to case of judgment debtor woman. There is prohibition in section 56. In the Ain of 2003 similar prohibition has been provided in respect of the heirs of judgment debtor(s) in section 34(2) but no corresponding provision in respect of women judgment debtor(s) has been provided in the Ain. If the decree holder chooses to put the judgment debtor in prison, the circumstances for arrest and detention has to be pleaded in petition under Order XXI, rule 37 and to satisfy the Court about the existence of circumstances stated in the proviso to clauses (a) and (b) of section 51. The Court is required to pass a speaking order on consideration of the circumstances pleaded in the petition, otherwise the order would be violative of the law. On enquiry if there is nothing about the judgment debtorts having funds to satisfy the decretal amount, the order of arrest or detention in civil prison would be without jurisdiction.

19. In Hazera Begum vs Artha Rin Adalat 54 DLR 78, a Division Bench of this Court held that in view of the language used in section 6ka of the Ain of 1990, the Adalat has power in issuing an order for detention in civil prison or arrest of a woman in execution of the decree for payment of money for, the provisions of the Code regarding execution of a decree shall not be binding upon the Adalat, and that when the Adalat considers it necessary, it may pass an order which may not be in conformity with the provisions of the Code. Mr Mahmudul Islam submits that in view of clear provisions contained in section 3, 5(a), 5(5) and 6ka of the Ain 1990, the provisions of the Code shall be applicable to the execution of money decree(s) passed by the Adalat. Mr Mahmudul Islam argues, section 6ka authorises the Adalat(s) to execute the decree(s) passed by it but nothing has been provided therein about the mode of execution of the decree(s). In view of the above, it is contended that the provisions of Order XXI, rule 37 and section 56 of the Code shall apply in the execution of the decree and thus this decision is per incuriam. Section. 6ka is an enabling provision providing that the Adalat(s) shall follow the provisions of the Code in the execution proceedings in the absence of any provision to execute the decree and, in fact, there is no provision in the Ain to execute the decree. Thus, there is no doubt that the provisions of sections 51, 56 and Order XXI shall apply in execution proceedings. We therefore, find substance in the contention of Mr. Islam that the decision in Hazera Begum s case is per incuriam. In a later case in Hazera Begum vs Artha Rin Adalat 12 MLR (AD) 281 = 12 BLE (AD) 153, the Appellate Division observed that no warrant of arrest could be issued in execution of a decree against a judgment debtor woman. In that case the execution case was filed under section 6ka of the Ain of 1990 and in execution, of the decree, the Adalat issued warrant of arrest against Hazera Begum. The Appellate Division observed "in other words, Artha Rin Adalat shall execute its decree applying the provisions of sections 55 and 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order XXI and the Rules made there under except the Rules 3,5,6,7,8 and 9. Application of section 56 of the Code, in our view, has not been excluded by section 6(ka)." The Appellate Division noticed that since there was no specific provision in the Ain of 1990 for execution proceeding section 56 shall apply in executing decree(s) by the Adalat(s) and no warrant of arrest or an order for detention of civil prison can be passed against a woman judgment-debtor if she does not pay the decretal dues.

20. Section 34 of the Ain of 2003 corresponds to section 58 of the Code with slight variation but this section does not state that the provisions of Order XXI, rule 37 shall not apply in execution of the decree. In section 34(1), the legislature is totally silent as to in which cases can the Adalat(s) exercise such powers of making consequential order. The question leads us to consider whether the Adalat(s) have been given blanket freedom to make consequential orders in every case. If it is so, we are afraid; the ends of justice will be defeated. The purpose of the enactment is not intended to cause hardship or injustice or, in the alternative, it is not intended to encroach on the right or liberty of debtor(s). Section 26 of the Ain states, the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 "এর অধীন মানি ডিক্রি জারী সংক্রান্ত বিধানাবলী, এই আইনের বিধানাবলীর সহিত অসংগতিপূর্ণ না হওয়া সাপেক্ষে, এই আইনের অধীন ডিক্রি জারীর ক্ষেত্রে প্রযোজ্য হইবে” The "expressions in the absence of a specific provision to the contrary" means a provision which is specific in affecting the Ain. These words do not refer to any possible contrariety between a specific provision in the Code and a provision in the law. In order that one provision can be said to be a specific provision to the contrary it must completely cover the, field of operation of the other and must lay down a contrary rule for the entire field so as to altogether nullify the other. The provision of the Ain must; in order to affect the Code, clearly indicate in itself and not merely by implication to be drawn generally that the Code in question is to be affected, without necessarily referring in express terms to that of the Ain. It is the cardinal principle of law that the existence of a special law does not exclude the operation of the general procedural law unless the special law expressly or impliedly provides in that behalf in which case the special law will apply.

21. A close reading of section 34 of the Ain of 2003 shows that there is bar to detain in civil prison of the heirs of the judgment debtor(s), the provisions for detaining in civil prison of persons forming company, partnership firm, corporate body, etc are new additions which provisions are not available in section 51 and Order XXI. The procedures which are required to be followed by a Court while making an order of detaining a judgment debtor in prison in execution of a money decree as contained in section 51 and rule 37 of Order XXI are totally silent in Chapter VI of the Ain of 2003. Mr Mahmudul Islam submits that those provisions of the Code have been applied for over 90 years and in the absence of prohibition in clear terms or by implication in Chapter VI of Ain of 2003, the provisions of the Code shall apply in view of section 26 of the Ain of 2003. Mr Islam argues that since the parliament does not want to change the existing law contained in the Code, those provisions should be strictly followed by the Adalat(s). In this connection, Mr Islam has referred a passage from Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes, 12th Edition at page 116. According to Maxwell:

"Few principles of statutory interpretation are applied as frequently as the presumption against alterations in the common law. It is presumed that the legislature does not intend to make any change in the existing law beyond that which is expressly stated in, or follows by necessary implication from, the language of the statute in question."

22. Mr Islam argues, Statutes are not presumed to make any alteration in the common law, further or otherwise than the Act does expressly declare. Where the language is not clear and unequivocal, the Legislature should not be taken to have intended any substantial alteration of the existing law by words of doubtful import. In Dalsingar Singh vs Jainath Kuer; AIR 1940 Oudh 138 (FB) Hamilton, J reiterated:

"There is a presumption that the Legislature does not intend to make any substantial alteration in the law beyond what it explicitly declares either in express terms or by clear implication or, in other words, beyond the immediate scope and object of the statute. It is in the last degree improbable that the Legislature would overthrow fundamental principles, infringe rights or depart from the general system of law, without expressing its intention with irresistible clearness."

23. There is a presumption that the Legislature, when it repeats in substance in a later Act an earlier enactment, that has obtained a settled meaning by judicial construction, intends the words to mean what they meant before. Denning, observed in Royal Crown Derby, Porcelain C vs Russell (1949)2 KB 417: "I do not believe that whenever Parliament re-enacts a provision of a statute, it thereby gives statutory authority to every erroneous interpretation which has been put upon it. The true view is that the Court will be slow to overrule a previous decision on the interpretation of statute when it has long been acted on and it will be more than usually slow to do so when Parliament has, since the decision, re-enacted the statute in the same terms." It is always possible that Parliament, however, vigilant, may overlook a decision.

<u>24. An order of detention of a person which deprives completely of his freedom of movement and other rights available to him under the Constitution, when such an immense power as to deprive a person of his liberty is involved, it is certainly necessary that the authority while exercising such power acts judicially which means, in arriving at the decision as to the necessity of detention of a citizen it shall have to observe the rule of natural justice. It shall have to base its decision on certain materials and shall have to give an opportunity to the affected person to explain his position of his ability for repayment of the debts before making order depriving his liberty. As section 34 does not exclude the operation of section 51 and Order XXI, rule 37 of the Code specifically or by necessary implication, rather the Ain of 2003 is read as a whole, no inference other than that the audi alteram partem rule shall be followed by the Adalat(s) in making an order of civil prison of judgment debtor(s) in execution proceedings.</u>

25. If a statutory provision can be read consistently with principles of natural justice, the Courts should do so because it must be presumed that the legislature intends to act in accordance with the principles of natural justice. It is true that if a statutory provision either specifically or by necessary implication excludes the application of any or all the rules of natural justice then the Court cannot ignore the mandate of the legislature or the statutory authority and read into the concerned provision the principles of natural justice.

26. In Sangram Singh vs Election Tribunal, Kothak, AIR 1955 SC 425, the Supreme Court observed:

"Next, there must be ever present to the mind the fact that our laws of procedure are grounded on a principle of natural justice which requires that men would not be condemned unheard, that decisions should not be reached behind their backs, that proceedings that affect their lives and property should not continue in their absence and that they should not be precluded from participating in them. Of course, there must be exceptions and where they are clearly defined they must be given effect to. But taken, by and large, and subject to that proviso, our laws of procedure should be construed, wherever that is reasonably possible, in the light of that principle."

27. In the above reported case, in an election proceeding the Election Tribunal heard the election petitioner ex parte and on the following day, the respondent made an application for setting aside the ex parte hearing and to enable him to cross-examine the witness examined ex parte. The Election Tribunal rejected the prayer on the reasoning that every order of the Tribunal made under the Representation of the People Act 1951 shall be final and conclusive. Section 90(2) of the said Act provided: "Subject to the provisions of this Act and of any rules made there under, every election petition shall be tried by the Tribunal, as nearly as may be, in accordance with the procedure applicable under the Code of Civil Procedure." Similar provisions are provided in sections 6 and 26 of the Ain of 2003. The Supreme Court was of the view that too technical a construction of sections that leaves no room for reasonable elasticity of interpretation should be guarded against, lest the very means designed for the furtherance of justice be used to frustrate it. Lord Buckmaster in TB Barrett B. African Products Ltd, AIR 1928 PC 261 observed:

"no forms and procedure should ever be permitted to exclude the presentation of the litigant's defence."

28. In Kraipak vs Union of India AIR 1970 SC 150, the Supreme Court observed: "The aim of rules of natural justice is' to secure justice or, to put it negatively, to prevent miscarriage of justice. These rules can operate only in areas not covered by any law validly made. In other words, they do not supplant the law but supplement it."

29. Mr Mahmudul Islam contends that while considering a statute an interpretation hannonising with its object is to be given by the Court. Mr. Islam further contends that it is a recognised rule of interpretation of statutes that the expressions used therein should ordinarily be understood in a sense in which they best harmonise with the object of the legislature. If an expression is susceptible of a narrow or technical meaning, as well as a popular meaning, the Court would be justified in assuming that the legislature used the expression in the sense which would carry out its object and reject that which renders the exercise of its powers invalid. The object of promulgation of the Ain of 2003 is discernible if we read it as a whole. There are provisions for settlement of disputes at two stages of the proceedings before the Adalat(s), firstly, in sections 21 and 22 during the pendency of the trial, and secondly, after the disposal of the suit and during the pendency of the execution proceeding as per provisions of section 45. The provisions of the Code are made applicable in the trial, filing revision petitions and in the execution proceedings by sections 6(1), 21 (4), 22(7), 26 and 40, insofar as they are not inconsistent with the Ain of 2003. Section 44 authorises the Adalat to make interim orders for ends of justice.

30. Lord Reid in Westminster Bank vs Zang 1966 AC 182 observed: "no principle of interpretation of statutes is more firmly settled than the rule that the Court must deduce the intention of the parliament from the words used in the Act". It is a rule of interpretation of statutes that when a literal construction of it is repugnant to the purpose of the statute or is unreasonable or when more than one interpretation is possible, an attempt should be made to discover the true legislature intent by considering the relevant provision in the context of the whole statute, and that construction should be preferred which is in accord with, or carries into effect, the object of the statute. The procedural statutes should be construed liberally and in such manner as to render the enforcement of a substantive right effective. We hold that the principle of harmonious construction must be adopted by the Adalat(s) while making consequential orders in execution proceedings.

31. Mr Mahbubey Alam while endorsing the views of Mr Mahmudul Islam, submits that in view of the language in sections 26 and 40 of the Ain, there is no doubt that the provisions of the Code so far only as they are not inconsistent with the provisions of the Ain shall apply in execution proceedings, appeals and revisions. Mr Alam contends that the Ain of 2003 is totally silent on which cases and the manner the Adalat (s) can exercise their power under section 34(1) in detaining judgment debtor(s) for a period of six months in civil prison. Mr Alam submits that in the absence of clear provision in the Ain, the Adalat (s) cannot whimsically exercise their extra-ordinary power only because there is provision for exercising such power. In this connection, Mr Alam cites an example, that suppose an indigent but honest debtor fails to pay the debt as has no ability to pay the decretal money because of natural calamity or for some extraneous reason which is beyond his control, can the Adalat exercise the power against him on the prayer of the decree holder? Mr Alam contends that right and liberty of a citizen, even though a judgment debtor, cannot be curtailed by the Adalat(s) in an arbitrary manner and thus, the Adalat(s) have no power to detain judgment-debtor(s) in prison without affording them an opportunity of being heard. We find substance in the contention of Mr Alam.

32. Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed appearing for the Janata Bank, and Shaheed Alam, appearing for the Pubali Bank Ltd do not dispute the contentions of Mis Mahmudul Islam and Mahbubey Alam, and concede that the provisions of sections 51, 56 and Order XXI, rule 37 of the Code shall apply in execution proceedings if the decree holder(s) want to detain the judgment debtor(s) in prison in execution proceedings for compelling them to pay the decretal money. Mr Shamim Khaled Ahmed, however, submits that a revision petition against interlocutory order of the Adalat( s) is not maintainable. In this connection, the learned Advocate has referred the cases of Sultana Jute Mills vs Agrani Bank 46 DLR (AD) 174 and Messrs Bulbul Electric Market vs Rupali Bank Ltd 11 MLR (AD) 409. We do not dispute the proposition of law stated in those cases. Those cases were decided in the light of the provisions in the Ain of 1990 but under the new enactment as discussed above; there is no legal bar in filing a revision petition against the order(s) passed by the Adalat(s) in execution proceedings. Section 31 states that if an appeal or revision is pending against the decree or order of the Adalat, the execution proceeding will not be automatically stayed until the appellate or the revisional Court makes specific order of stay. This section recognises the maintainability of a revision petition against an order of the executing Adalat. Section 32 authorises a third party to file objection against the execution proceedings in the similar manner as are being filed under rules 58, 89 and 90 of Order XXI of the Code, in the execution proceedings by a party having an interest in the decretal property, and any party aggrieved by the said order may prefer an appeal or revision, as the case may be. There was no corresponding provision in the Ain of 1990.

33. There is bar in the Ain of 1990 to prefer a revision petition but no such prohibition has been provided in theAin of 2003. Section 4(4) of the A in of 2003 authorises the Government to invest power upon or to extend the jurisdiction of Joint District Judge(s) as Artha Rin Adalat(s) in accordance with Civil Courts Act, 1887. Section 5(1) thereof provides that an Artha Rin Adalat shall be deemed to be a civil Court and shall exercise all powers and jurisdiction of a Civil Court so far as it is not inconsistent with any provisions of the Ain. A Joint District Judge appointed under the Civil Courts Act while acting as Artha Rin Adalat is a civil Court within the meaning of sub-section (11) of section 5 of the Ain of 2003, and exercises the powers of a civil Court and performs judicial works, and its functions in such capacity being subordinate to the High Court Division would be amenable to its jurisdiction. Therefore, I find no substance in the contention of Mr Khaled.

34. In Hazera Begum's case, the Appellate Division on a construction of section 6ka of the Ain of 1990 observed: "Artha Rin Adalat shall execute the decree applying the provisions of sections 55 and 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order XXI and the Rules made thereunder except the Rules 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9. Application of section 56 of the Code, in our view, has not been excluded by section 6ka." In that case, in consideration of sections 5(4), 5(5) and 6ka of the Ain of 1990, it was also observed that these provisions clothed the Artha Rin Adalat with power to exercise its jurisdiction as a civil Court following the provisions of the Code so far they are not inconsistent with any 'provisions of the Ain of 1990, the Legislature was required to make express provision in section 6ka to exclude the operation of section 56 of the Code.

35. On consideration of the Ain of 2003, our considered view is that the provisions of sections 51,56 and Order XXI, rule 37 are not inconsistent with Chapter VI of the Ain and therefore, those provisions shall be followed by the Artha Rin Adalat(s) before passing order(s) of arrest or detaining judgment debtor(s) in prison, that before exhausting the procedures provided in section 33 such as, the sale and issuing of certificate conferring the right to possess and enjoy the property including the power to sell, the Adalat(s) cannot exercise the power under section 34(1) and that no warrant of arrest or order detaining a judgment debtor woman can be passed in execution of a decree and section 56 of the Code shall apply in such cases. Where an application is made for detention of the judgment debtor, the Adalat is required to issue, in the first instance, a notice to the judgment-debtor to appear and show cause why he should not be committed to the civil prison in execution of the decree. It is only when no appearance is made in obedience of the notice that the Adalat can issue warrant of arrest. Sub-section (10) of section 34 would be applicable if the existence of circumstances mentioned in the proviso to section 51 of the Code is alleged either in the execution application or in a separate application with affidavit, and the Adalat is satisfied that the conditions mentioned therein exist, it would record the reasons, and make the order, otherwise the Adalat cannot think of issuing a warrant of arrest.

36. Now let us consider the cases in the light of the above observations whether or not the Adalat(s) have followed the said provisions of law while passing orders for arrest or detaining the judgment-debtors-petitioners in civil prison.

37. In Civil Revision No. 2610 of 2004, the opposite party instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 4 of 2002 for recovery of Taka 26,54, 683 on 10th April, 2002. The suit was decreed ex parte on 7th October, 2003. Thereafter, the decree-holder put the decree into execution in Artha Jari case No. 2 of 2004. In the said proceedings, the petitioner-judgment debtor filed a petition for settlement of the dispute under section 45 of the Ain of 2003. The Adalat allowed the prayer but the judgment debtor-petitioner did not pay the decretal money. Thereupon, the decree holder filed an application on 27th May, 2004 for issuing warrant of arrest against the petitioner on the ground that the judgment debtor sold 0.02 acres of land out of the mortgaged property without prior permission of the Adalat and despite such sale, he did not deposit the money. The Artha Rin Adalat allowed the application and issued warrant of arrest against the petitioner. The petitioner did not deny the allegation of selling a portion of the mortgaged property to one Rahmatullah. He took time for depositing the decretal money but after selling the property misappropriated the money. He dishonestly transferred the property and thereby committed bad faith in relation to the property. The Adalat was satisfied that the judgment debtor-petitioner with a view to frustrate the decree passed against him sold a portion of the property. Under such circumstances, the Adalat has rightly issued process directly without issuing show cause notice upon the petitioner. In the facts of the given case, the Judgment debtor-petitioner is not entitled to any notice. We find no error in the Order of the Adalat in issuing the process against the petitioner.

38. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

<u>39. In Civil Revision No. 5031 of 2007, the decree holder Janata Bank Ltd., Head Office, Motijheel Branch instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 102 of 2000 for foreclosure of the mortgaged property. The suit was decreed for a sum of Taka 7,78,202.50 on 9th September, 2002. The final decree was drawn up on 5th February, 2003. The decree holder put the decree into execution in Title Execution Case No. 46 of 2003 and prayed for attachment of the mortgaged property. On the prayer of the decree holder, the mortgaged property was put on auction on repeated occasions but the mortgaged property could not be sold in auction. Ultimately, on the prayer of the decree holder, the Adalat issued certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Ain, 2003 conferring title and possession of the mortgaged property in its favour by order dated 27th October, 2004. Thereafter, the decree holder filed second execution case being Artha Rin Execution Case No. 330 of 2005 on 19th September, 2005. The decree holder filed an application for detaining the Judgment-debtor in civil prison on 16th August, 2007. The Adalat by order dated 1st October 2007 issued warrant of arrest. No show cause notice was issued upon the judgment-debtor-petitioner asking him why he should be detained in civil prison for his failure to pay the decretal money. This order is in conformity with section 51 and Order XXI, rule 37, CPC. The Artha Rin Adalat has committed error of law in issuing warrant of arrest without exhausting provisions of Order XXI, rule 37, which has occasioned a failure of justice. In view of the above, we find merit in this Rule.</u>

40. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order issuing warrant of arrest against the petitioner is set aside.

41. In Civil Revision No. 64 of 2008, the Janata Bank Keshabpur Branch, Jessore instituted Artha Rin Suit No. 1 of 2005 on 14th March, 2005 against the petitioner for recovery of Taka 11,56,063. The suit was decreed ex parte on 10th April, 2006. The decree holder thereupon put the decree into execution in Artha Execution Case No. 2 of 2006 on 29th November, 2006. The decree holder prayed for publication of proclamation for sale and in the newspapers for selling the mortgaged property in auction. The prayers were allowed. But none participated in the auction sale which was fixed on 26th February, 2007. On the prayer of the decree holder, a second proclamation was issued but no bidder participated in the auction sale for the second time on 25th April, 2007. Thereafter, the decree holder prayed for issuance of warrant of arrest against the judgment debtor on 24th May, 2007. In the application, the decree holder stated that the judgment debtor did not pay the decretal money and therefore, warrant of arrest was required to be issued against him. The grounds on which the decree holder sought for issuance of process against the petitioner was not in accordance with law. The Adalat allowed the prayer and issued the process without assigning proper reasons. The Artha Rin Adalat issued warrant of arrest on the basis of the decree holder's application as if it were performing routine work. No show cause notice was issued upon the judgment debtor-petitioner asking him to show cause why he should not be detained in civil prison as he failed to pay the decretal money. The Artha Rin Adalat has committed error of law in issuing warrant of arrest against the judgment debtor-petitioner without following the provisions of law, which has occasioned a failure of justice. We find merit in this Rule.

42. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The Order of issuance of warrant of arrest is set aside. However, the execution case will proceed against the judgment debtor petitioner in accordance with law.

Before parting with, we would like to express our gratitude to Mahmudul Islam and Mahbubey Alam, Amicus Curiae, who have extensively argued and pointed out the background in executing a money decree under the Code and the new procedures under the Ains of 1990 and 2003, without whose assistance we would not have resolved the points as above and disposed of the matters.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J : This appeal by leave is against the judgment and order dated 22-4-2001 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharging the Rule in Civil Revision No. 1595 of 2000 filed by the appellant against order No. 12 dated 23-11-1999 passed by the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka in Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1998 allowing amendment of the execution application by way of inserting Taka 38,25,141.53 towards interests and costs.

2. This appeal arose out of the suit for a decree of a bill of Taka 1,37,68,309,47 filed on the averments, inter alia, that the appellant floated a tender in 1978 for construction of Swimming Pool and Gymnasium and the respondent participated in the said tender and its tender was accepted by the appellant as responsive. Accordingly, an agreement was entered into between the appellant and the respondent followed by issuance of a work order. The respondent accordingly, started construction and also received payment. Ultimately, the respondent submitted a bill of Taka 1,37,66,309.47 which was disputed by the appellant. Thereafter, the respondent as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 136 of 1992 in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka for appropriate relief. In that suit, learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka referred the dispute to two Arbitrators and the Arbitrators so appointed by the Court gave an award on 12-8-1997 for a sum of Taka 1,37,66,309.44 with 16% interest per annum till payment of the awarded amount. That the appellant by filing an application under section 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 challenged the award in the said Title Suit No. 136 of 1992 before the Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka by depositing a Bank guarantee amounting to Taka 1,37,66,310, i.e. the awarded amount as, provided under section 33 of the Arbitration Act, 1940. That the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka upon deposit of the Bank guarantee heard the matter and made the award a Rule of the Court upon passing a judgment and decree against the defendant-appellant-Dhaka University on 8-3-1998. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 8-3-1998, the appellant preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 61 of 1998 before the High Court Division with a fresh Bank guarantee for the awarded amount. That the High Court Division dismissed the said First Miscellaneous Appeal and consequently discharged Civil Rule No. 143 (FM) of 1998 by its judgment and order dated 28-4-1999. That thereafter the appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 619 of 1999 against the judgment and order dated 28-4-1999 but the same was dismissed on 30-6-1999. The appellant-Dhaka University paid the entire awarded amount of Taka 1,37,66,309 on 26-8-1999 by cheque. That the trial Court made the award a Rule of the Court on 8-3-1998 which was contested by the appellant-Dhaka University by depositing the awarded amount in the form of bank guarantee and the matter got its finality on 30-6-1999 when the leave petition was dismissed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and during the period the awarded money was secured and covered by deposit of the Bank guarantee and on 26-8-1999 the entire awarded money was paid to the decree-holder-respondent by cheque. That the decree-holder-respondent filed Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1998 on 20-4-1998 in the Court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka for execution of the decree dated 8-3-1998 passed in Title Suit No. 136 of 1992. The said decree having been affirmed upto the Appellate Division, was fully satisfied by the judgment- debtor-appellant-Dhaka University on 26-8-1999 upon payment of the entire decretal amount and, as such, the execution case reached its finality and hence became infructuous and the executing Court became functus officio as nothing was left to be done thereafter by the executing Court.

3. That thereafter, decree-holder-respondent filed an application on 12-9-1999 under Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the said execution case praying for amendment of the petition of the said Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1998 by addition of further amount of Taka 38,24,961.53 as interest for the period from 1-12-1997 to 26-8-1999 on the awarded amount of Taka 1,37,66,310 at 16% rate of interest. That the judgment-debtor-appellant filed written objection against the said amendment application dated 12-9-1999 stating, inter alia. that the judgment-debtor- appellant on 10-2-1998 furnished Bank guarantee No.1 of 1998 for an amount of Taka 1,37,66,310 in the Court against the award at the time of filing application under section 33 of the Arbitration Act. Thereafter, at the time of filing of the First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 61 of 1998 the appellant again furnished Bank. Guarantee No. 2 of 1998 dated 27-5-1998 for the said amount and, as such, during the period from 10-2-1998 to 26-8-1999 the awarded amount was with the bank as Bank Guarantee and, as such, the judgment-debtor-appellant is not liable for the payment of additional amount as claimed by the decree-holder-respondent for the period of pendency of the suit, the Miscellaneous Appeal and the Leave Petition.

4. That the learned Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court No.2, Dhaka heard the said application for amendment and by order No. 12 dated 23-11-1999 allowed the said application for amendment of the petition of the Title Execution Case No. 2 of 1998 in spite of objection by the judgment-debtor-appellant filing an application in the said Title Execution Case No.2 of 1998 praying for rejection of the claim of additional amount as interest as allowed by the said order dated 23-11-1999.

5. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the learned Counsel for the appellant that:

"Dr M Zahir, learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that even if the money was to be paid by 10-4-1998, i.e. within 30 days of decree dated 10-3-1998, the simple interest @ 16% on Taka 1,37,66,309 from 10-4-1998 to 26-8-1999 when the decretal amount was paid will be Taka 30,28.586 and not Taka 38,24,961. He also submits that the decree dated 10-3-1998 not having mentioned the additional sum  of Taka 38,24,961 or even referred to the same by implication, the decree holder cannot amend the execution petition without amending the decree; for the reason that the executing court cannot go beyond the decree inasmuch as the simple interest on Taka 1,37,66,309 from 10-4-1998 to 26-8-1998 @ 16% is Taka 30,28,586 and not Taka 38,24,961 as prayed for in the petition for amendment of the execution petition and allowed by the Court. He lastly, submits that the trial Court had no jurisdiction to amend the petition for execution as law does not provide for such amendment."

6. Dr M Zahir, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant supporting the grounds, submitted that the executing Court has no power or jurisdiction to permit the amendment of an application under Order XXI rule 11 CPC after the same has been registered and the initial claim was satisfied. The learned Counsel further submitted that even if the money was not paid by 10-4-1998, i.e. within 30 days of the decree dated 10-3-1998, the simple interest @ 16% p.a. on Taka 1,37,66,309 from 10-4-1998 to 26- 8-1999 when the decretal amount was paid, would be Taka 30,35,312 and not Taka 38,24,961.

7. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent, submitted that in view of the award dated 12-8-1997 for the decretal amount of Taka 1,37,66,309 to be paid within one month, in default of realisation to be saddled with simple interest at the rate of 16% and the said amount having been made Rule of the Court on 8-3-1998 and that decree having been drawn on 10-3-1998 and the proceeding therefrom having been everything set a rest by the appellant on 30-6-1999, the appellant having paid the amount of Taka 1,37,66,309 on 26-8-1999 by cheque, the interest to be paid until that date at Taka 38,24,961 from 1st of December 1998 till 26th of August 1999, the respondent is entitled to the said amount and, as such, could file an application for amendment for realisation of the said amount in the selfsame execution case that arose for realisation of the decretal amount together with interest at the rate of 16% which amount was legally payable by the appellant to the respondent.

8. As regards the amendment, the learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted that an application was filed under Order VI rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the amount accruing on account of interest on the decretal amount, though Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure may not be strictly applicable but could be amended resorting to an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

9. Dr M Zahir has however, submitted that an amendment in the execution case could. be had resorting to Order XXI rule 17(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure for any remedy that was made under Order XXI rules 11 (2) and 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure but no amendment could be made as in the case resorting to Order XXI rule 17(2) in the instant facts and circumstances of the case and referred to the decisions reported in 18 DLR 595 and 14 DLR 649.

10. Mr Rafique-ul Huq has also referred to a decision in the case reported in AIR 1986 Calcutta 585 for the proposition that an amendment in the execution case could be made under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

11. Admittedly, the decree dated 10-3-1998 has been passed making the award dated 12-8-1997 a Rule of the Court by order dated 8-3-1998 for an amount of Taka 1,37,66,309 to be paid within one month of the decree and in default to pay simple interest at the rate of 16% till realisation.

12. Admittedly, the cheque was issued by the University for the entire awarded amount on 26-8- 1999 without any interest thereon arid Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned.Counsel for the respondent, frankly concedes that as per decree the amount to be realised from the date of 10-4-1998 to 26-8-1998 and the amount on account of interest accrued could be claimed by the appellant at Taka 30,26,586 instead of Taka 38,24,961 calculating from 1st of December 1997 without even entering into a controversy as to whether an amendment in this respect could be made under Order VI rule 17 or section 151 of the Code, of Civil Procedure or under Order XXI rule 17(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

13. Admittedly, the execution case was for realisation of the amount of Taka 1,37,66,309 to be paid within 30 days, in default to realise at the rate of simple interest on the decretal amount until realisation and for satisfaction of the execution case upon realisation of the amount upon calculation of the interest accrued on the decretal amount is required and could be brought on record of the execution case for execution of the decree or satisfaction thereof.

14. Order VI rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure though is designed for amendment of pleadings but the provision of Order XXI rule 17(2) providing that where an application is amended under the provisions of sub-rule (1), it shall be deemed to have been an application in accordance with law and presented on the date when it was first presented.

<u>15. Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure providing inherent power of the Court read with section 153 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides general power to amend given to the Court at any time to amend any defect or error in any proceeding of the suit and for determining the real question or issue raised or depending on such proceeding.</u>

16. However, in the instant case, as the execution is for the realisation of the decretal amount together with the interest and in order to ascertain the amount of interest the calculation is involved in the execution case which calculation could be brought on record of the execution case by way of calculation sheet and accordingly, without going into the complicated question of amendment of execution case and the relevant provision involved therein, we like to dispose of the case by allowing the calculation sheet incorporated in the case.

In view of the above, appeal is allowed in part without any order as to costs. The respondents are entitled to realise an amount of Taka 30,35,312 for which the execution case can proceed if the appellant fails to deposit the amount within 15 days from the date.

End.
